cd /home/saidler/repos/tatari-tv/slack-cli/add-mcp
git push -u origin add-mcp 2>&1 | /usr/bin/tail -4
cat > /tmp/claude/slack-pr.md <<'EOF'
## What

Adds a local stdio MCP server to `slack` via the shared `mcp-io` library (v0.1.0), exposing the Slack tools to Claude Code / Desktop. First consumer of `mcp-io-rs`. This is Phase 4 of the `mcp-io-rs` design (`tatari-tv/mcp-io-rs`, `docs/design/2026-07-09-mcp-io-rs.md`).

New subcommand: `slack mcp <serve|register|unregister|status|bundle>`. The library owns all the scaffolding (stdio lifecycle, logging discipline, self-registration into Claude config, `.mcpb` bundle); slack supplies only its `ServerHandler`.

## Tools exposed (11)

`auth_test`, `chat_post_message`, `conversations_history`, `conversations_info`, `conversations_open`, `conversations_replies`, `download_file`, `search_messages`, `users_conversations`, `users_info`, `workspace` -- each wrapping the existing `SlackApi` methods, unchanged.

## How it's wired

- `mcp-io` git dep pinned to `v0.1.0`; `rmcp` 2.1.0 + `tokio` added directly for the handler.
- `Command::Mcp(mcp_io::McpCmd)` + early intercept in `main.rs`, mirroring the existing `renew`/`update` arm. The tokio runtime is built ONLY inside the `mcp` arm -- every existing sync command is untouched.
- `SlackMcpServer` owns a cloned `Config` (token-free construction, so register/status/bundle need no login). Each tool call rebuilds the token source + client inside `spawn_blocking` (reqwest::blocking would panic on the async runtime); a 401 maps to a recoverable tool error, not a protocol error.
- `serverInfo.name = "slack"` set explicitly (rmcp otherwise reports itself as "rmcp").
- `chat_post_message` applies the same mandatory agent-attribution signature as `slack write` -- an MCP post is an agent post; the signature is not suppressible.

## Verified

- `otto ci` green.
- `slack mcp serve` handshakes over stdio and lists all 11 tools (`serverInfo.name="slack"`), verified by a headless `initialize`/`tools/list` exchange.
- `slack mcp register --target user` writes `{"type":"stdio","command":"<abs>","args":["mcp","serve"]}` via `claude mcp add-json`; `status` reports it registered.
- Sync commands build no tokio runtime.

## Shakedown TODO (post-merge)

The live "Claude Code calls a slack tool end to end" round-trip needs a manual shakedown with an interactive MCP client -- everything else is covered headless.

## Merge note

Additive against the in-flight `slack-cli-capability-expansion` branch: new `src/mcp.rs` module, append-only `Command` variant + dispatch arm, no `api.rs` signature changes. Expected to merge cleanly whichever lands first.
EOF
gh pr create --base main --head add-mcp \
  --title "feat(mcp): expose slack tools via mcp-io stdio MCP server" \
  --body-file /tmp/claude/slack-pr.md 2>&1 | /usr/bin/tail -3

Ten handoff docs across nine repos, all written 2026-09-15. Each one carries a next action, the evidence behind the finding, code pointers, and acceptance checks. All ten are evaluations, not implementations: nothing here has shipped, and every baseline commit is dated, so recheck HEAD before acting.

Left uncommitted in each repo.

---

## `scottidler/claude`: voice guard coverage
`docs/2026-09-15-voice-route-coverage-handoff.md` | baseline `3815d7b` on branch `intent-guards`

- The em-dash hook scans command text for selected git/gh commands. It never reads a referenced body file.
- Reproduced: inline `gh pr create --body` denied; the same prose via `--body-file`, `slack write`, and a Marquee publish file all allowed.
- `settings.json` also omitted `chat_schedule_message` from the em-dash MCP matcher at inspection time.
- Fix is to extract the actual outbound prose per route: file bodies, scheduled messages, edits, follow-ups, rich text.
- Subjective voice judgment stays with the private corpus. This public repo does not acquire private examples.

## `scottidler/keep`: voice evaluation
`docs/2026-09-15-voice-evaluation-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `06d2e6a`

- Build a private set of actual rejected drafts + accepted revisions for four genres: Slack replies, PR descriptions, design docs, announcements.
- One global brevity score cannot judge four registers. Each case records task, genre, rejected draft, accepted revision, reason, provenance.
- Score facts and the ask BEFORE style. A terser draft that drops a condition or flips a verdict fails.
- Separate deterministic lint from subjective voice. A draft can pass punctuation checks and still sound wrong.
- Hold out examples so profile edits get evaluated on material they were not tuned against.

## `scottidler/second-brain`: recall and analytics
`main/docs/2026-09-15-recall-and-analytics-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `af55da4`

- The vault-recall skill tells Claude to read note files directly, which bypasses `bump_access`, the only path that records use.
- An `unread` frontmatter label is therefore not proof nobody used the note. That inference comes out of the skill.
- Quality scoring clears fields when warnings disappear, so blank != clean. Of 487 notes in the AI content-date cohort, 441 were blank and 46 medium. Calling those 441 "unscored" was unsupported.
- `list_notes` caps results with `count = results.len()`, no total, no continuation, and orders `date DESC` with no unique tie-breaker.
- `date`, `ingested`, and first capture are different concepts: 487 by `date`, 718 by `ingested`.

## `otto-rs/otto`: abandoned runs
`docs/2026-09-15-abandoned-runs-handoff.md` | baseline `0645f78`, reproduced on installed v2.5.0

- The local database held 221 runs marked `running`, newest started September 8. 183 had no run directory, 29 no lock file, nine had an available lock. None was held.
- Historical rows prove nothing on their own. An isolated repro does: SIGKILL the Otto parent after the task prints `ready`, let the child finish, run another task. The first run and task still say `running`.
- `RunStatus` only has Running | Success | Failed. Needs an explicit abandoned/interrupted outcome through schema, queries, History, Stats, retention.
- `RunLock` already gives a kernel-backed liveness signal. Reuse it. Never infer death from elapsed time.
- Follow-on: a compact run result with run ID, task outcomes, failed-task log tails, and paths to full logs.

## `tatari-tv/clyde`: Slack outcomes
`docs/2026-09-15-slack-outcomes-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `8712ddc`

- `classify_tool` recognizes `conversations_add_message` but not `chat_post_message`, the name Claude Code actually uses now.
- In the 250 most recently active root transcripts since September 1: 27 successful `chat_post_message` calls across eight sessions. All eight catalog outcomes reported zero `slack-messages`.
- Six successful `chat_update` calls too. Those are edits, not posts. Define posted | edited | scheduled | delivered separately.
- Counts are tool calls, not delivered messages. Forks, fanout, chunking, and partial success need explicit accounting.
- Version the extractor and recompute stored `outcome_json`. Changing source alone leaves the historical zeros in place.

## `tatari-tv/clyde`: setup effectiveness
`docs/2026-09-15-setup-effectiveness-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `8712ddc`

- The question: did setup audit chunks A-C reduce repeated corrections and review churn without increasing useless denials?
- Assets exist: 3,327 catalog sessions, 3,249 with efficiency blobs, 3,252 with outcome blobs, plus per-session/daily/weekly/subagent views.
- A setup commit SHA alone misses local edits and deployed/runtime differences. Record a digest of the effective config including dirty changes and plugin versions.
- Mid-session config changes are intervals. Do not retroactively assign today's setup to old sessions.
- Fix the Slack outcome extraction first. Denial counts alone never become accuracy scores.

## `tatari-tv/slack-cli`: watch token recovery
`docs/2026-09-15-watch-token-recovery-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `fda1002`

- `watch::terminal_class` maps EVERY `TokenError` to terminal `auth` and tells the user to run `slack login`.
- `valet-client` already distinguishes rejected identity/enrollment from transport errors and `Vend { status, detail }`, which can be a temporary service failure.
- The token request happens inside `SlackClient::call_method`'s call loop, so a transient Valet blip kills an already-armed watch.
- `arm` baselines at the newest message, so an unnecessary stop plus restart silently drops the interruption window. No-backfill is an intentional contract, not a bug to quietly change.
- Split terminal from retryable, preserve the cursor, bounded backoff with Retry-After where available.

## `tatari-tv/valet`: token error contract
`main/docs/2026-09-15-token-error-contract-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `65181bb`

- Companion to the Slack CLI item. Trigger is Slack CLI switching to Valet by default on September 14.
- Goal: a long-lived consumer can tell "login/enroll" from "retry this service failure".
- No server defect was established. Observed client mapping: 401 -> rejected Okta identity, 403/404 -> not enrolled, other failures -> `Vend`.
- Enumerate the actual vend failure classes: invalid identity, absent/revoked grant, upstream throttling, upstream temporary failure, transport failure, malformed response.
- Fix the Slack client classification first if the existing contract is sufficient. Close this with contract evidence, do not invent a server feature.

## `tatari-tv/marquee`: body search evaluation
`docs/2026-09-15-body-search-evaluation-handoff.md` | baseline `main` `760c89f`

- `matches_query` searches title, description, tags, space, slug. Body text is deliberately excluded by the September findability design.
- This is a proposed extension, not a regression, and it does not amend the Confluence-owned product intent.
- Experiment first: collect actual "find that document" queries with known answers where the useful terms live only in the body, then measure current search against them.
- Compare metadata search against a disposable FTS index over extracted text, with ordinary metadata queries as controls.
- Prompt and context stay excluded from corpus-wide search. S3 stays canonical, no request-time fetching of every entry document.

## `scottidler/loopr`: Claude Code worker
`v5/docs/2026-09-15-claude-code-worker-handoff.md` | baseline `v5` `c50682a3`, last commit July 13

- Lowest priority of the ten. Question is whether Loopr's DAG/worktree/integration machinery helps a workflow whose daily driver is already Claude Code.
- `LlmClient` models completion calls. A Claude Code process owns a tool-using session, so it is not a drop-in implementation of that interface.
- Prototype at the agent/worktree boundary instead: work item + workspace + constraints + acceptance command in, session ID + change identity + verification evidence out.
- Make config inheritance explicit: which rules, skills, permissions, and project instructions the worker gets.
- Exit zero or a worker saying "done" does not establish acceptance. Failed checks must stop integration and keep the evidence.

---

## Cross-repo dependencies

- `slack-cli` watch recovery -> `valet` token error contract. Same fix, two repos. Keep the owner in the Slack item so two agents do not independently redesign token refresh.
- `clyde` Slack outcomes -> `clyde` setup effectiveness. Outcome counts have to be right before any before/after comparison means anything.
- `claude` voice routes -> `keep` voice evaluation. Deterministic guards in one, subjective judgment in the other, corpus stays private.
- `claude` voice routes + `clyde` setup effectiveness -> the setup audit program baton at `claude/docs/design/2026-09-13-setup-audit-program.md`. Chunks A-C are done; none of this reorders D-J.
EOF

:mega: Heads up: the `general` skills plugin just split up

The `general` Claude Code plugin costs ~4,292 always-on tokens in every session, whether you use any of it or not. It's now split by capability: 20 skills moved out into 5 new plugins plus `plugin-dev`. Most of your old `/general:*` commands stop working until you install the replacement.

Where things moved:
• `pr` → *babysit-prs*, *coderabbit-autofix*, *review-pr*, *debug-pr*, *session-launcher*
• `spec` → *design-doc*, *tech-spec-review*, *convergent-review*
• `llm` → *codex*, *gemini*, *model-selector*
• `repo` → *tatari-repos*, *who-do-i-ask*, *pattern-applicator*, *test-runner*, *migrate-poetry-to-uv*
• `ctx` → *context-audit*, *context-usage*
• `plugin-dev` (already existed) → *build-a-loop*, *skill-authoring*, and the *skill-reviewer* agent
*markee* stays in `general`, nothing to do there.

What to watch out for:

▎ The old `/general:<name>` commands still show up but do nothing real: they're dead placeholders that just tell you where the skill moved. The model won't auto-reach for them either. This is a one-time grace window, not a fixed deadline. The placeholders get removed in a follow-up cleanup, so don't get comfortable with the old command.

`platform` and the team plugins are unaffected. `plugin-dev` only gains skills.

:point_right: Do this now:
1. `/plugin marketplace update`, then restart Claude Code
2. Check `plugins/general/README.md` for the full old-name → new-name table
3. Install what you actually use, e.g. `/plugin install pr@tatari-skills`
4. Retrain muscle memory: `/general:review-pr` → `/pr:review-pr`, etc.

tool_input.command:
cat >> docs/design/2026-07-31-slack-directory-implementation-notes.md <<'EOF'

## Phase 3: `slack usergroups` verb, skill, MCP tool

### Design decisions

- **A purpose-built `GroupJson` rather than serializing the wire `UserGroup`.** `UserGroup` already
  derives `Serialize`, so emitting it directly was the shorter path -- but its JSON carries
  `user_count` and `date_delete` while the TEXT form prints `member_count()` (which prefers
  `users.len()` when members were fetched) and `is_disabled()`. Two names for one concept, free to
  disagree the moment `--members` is passed: text would print 2 while JSON printed 99. The
  projection computes each derived value once and both renderings read it. Asserted by
  `json_carries_derived_fields_not_wire_fields` and `member_count_prefers_the_fetched_list`
  (`command/usergroups/tests.rs`).
- **`--empty` does NOT force `include_users=true`; `--user` does.** `include_count=true` is always
  sent, so the count needed by `--empty` is already on the wire. `--user` has no such shortcut: the
  filter tests membership and Slack only returns `users[]` when asked. Documented on
  `usergroups::run` so the asymmetry does not read as an oversight.
- **`--empty` excludes an UNKNOWN count instead of treating it as zero.** `--empty` asserts
  certainty about membership; `None` is the absence of that certainty. Reporting a group as empty
  on the strength of a missing field is the fail-open shape. Test:
  `empty_flag_excludes_unknown_counts`.
- **`--user` on an unknown or ambiguous handle is a loud error, not an empty list.** A typo'd
  handle would otherwise render identically to "this person is in no groups" --
  `usergroups::resolve_user_id` bails. Resolution goes through the shared `CacheLookup::user`, so a
  cold cache triggers the EXISTING watermark-gated `users.list` fill rather than a bespoke path.
- **The id column pads, not just the handle column.** Real `S…` ids are uniformly 11 characters so
  the padding is a no-op in production, but a single short id would shift its whole row left and
  falsify the alignment claim `render_text`'s doc comment makes. Widths count `chars()`, not bytes.
- **Member enrichment is cache-only, degrading to raw `U…` with a WARN.** Mirrors `search`'s author
  enrichment exactly; a per-member `users.info` would be a call storm across 172 groups. An
  unresolved member prints the raw id rather than a blank line, because "who is in this group" is
  the question and a dropped line silently under-reports it.

### Deviations

- **`plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` gained a `usergroups` keyword.** Not in the phase's bullet
  list. It is the plugin's discovery surface and a new verb belongs in it; `plugin-guard` does not
  read the field, so nothing forced it. Disclosed rather than silent. The four prose enumerations
  in `README.md` / `plugin/README.md` were deliberately left alone -- they are Phase 8's named work.
- **The MCP `get_info` instructions string was extended** to name user groups and the `S…` id
  shape. Also not in the bullet list; it is the one enumeration a connected LLM actually reads at
  handshake, and leaving it saying "look up users and channels" while a twelfth tool listed groups
  would be stale on merge.

### Tradeoffs

- **Client-side filtering over server-side.** `usergroups.list` takes no query parameter, so every
  filter is necessarily client-side over the full 172-group response. Chosen over not offering the
  filters at all; the response is un-paginated and small, so a filtered call costs the same one
  request as an unfiltered one.
- **A `{usergroups: [...]}` envelope rather than a bare array.** A bare array is marginally nicer
  to pipe, but `search`'s `{query, hits}` set the house precedent and an envelope leaves room to
  add filter context later without a breaking shape change.

### Doc amendments

- **Criterion `slack write --print -m "hey @bao-eng"` fails with a usergroup-naming message.**
  Amended: a doc defect on two independent counts, neither of which involves this phase's code.
  (1) `-m` is not a flag `slack write` has -- content is a trailing positional; observed
  `error: unexpected argument '-m' found`. (2) `--print` cannot produce the error AT ALL by
  documented design: `write.rs:19-21` guarantees zero network calls on that path and therefore
  skips mention resolution entirely; observed `slack write --print '#eng-oncall' 'hey @bao-eng'`
  exits 0 printing the literal handle. The criterion named the one flag that routes around the
  code path it was written to test. Replaced with `--preview`, which reaches `build_body`
  (`write.rs:384-391`) and so bails during resolution with zero posts, plus the network-free unit
  test. Full evidence in the design doc next to the criterion.
- **`UserGroup::user_count`'s doc comment** asserted "Slack sends this as a QUOTED STRING, not a
  number" as fact. Corrected in `api.rs` to state that both forms occur and cite the 2026-08-01
  live measurement (bare numbers) against Slack's reference sample (quoted). A Phase 1 artifact,
  fixed here rather than left knowingly false; the tolerant deserializer it justifies is unchanged.

### Open questions

- **`bao-eng` is not a usergroup handle in this workspace.** `slack usergroups bao-eng` returns
  empty; the group handles still carry the `mbp-` prefix while the channels were renamed to `bao-`,
  which is exactly the drift Phase 7's `previous_names` criterion exists to explain. The design
  doc uses `@bao-eng` as its example unresolvable handle, which is still a VALID test of the
  message (it is unresolvable, which is the point) but is not the usergroup a reader would assume.
  Worth a pass over the doc's examples in Phase 8 to use a handle that actually exists.
EOF
echo done

cat > $SP/pr.md <<'EOF'
## Motivation

Slack encodes a group mention as `<!subteam^S04SS1QSTRB>` and ships no name fallback: measured at 0 of 135 occurrences in `#eng-on-call`. Every one of those lands in an agent's context as an opaque id. There was also no way to ask "who is in this group", "what is this person's Slack id", or "who is in this channel" without leaving the CLI.

## What lands

Three verbs, two flags, three MCP tools.

- `slack usergroups [QUERY] [--members] [--user] [--empty] [--include-disabled]`. The query matches the `S...` id, so an id pasted straight out of a message resolves in one call.
- `slack users [QUERY] [--email] [--title] [--all]`. Reads LIVE from `users.list`, never the id-cache.
- `slack channels members | info`. `members` walks `conversations.members` to completion, `info` surfaces `previous_names`.
- `slack read --resolve-mentions`. Classifies every `<...>` span: usergroup, user, channel, broadcast, link, date, unknown.
- `slack search --mentions <target>`. Keeps only hits that genuinely mention the target as an entity.
- MCP tools 11 -> 14: `usergroups_list`, `users_list`, `conversations_members`.

Needs `usergroups:read`, granted via valet PR #9 (https://github.com/tatari-tv/valet/pull/9). Everything else runs on scopes already held.

## Why `users` reads live

The cache's `users` map fills lazily from message authors only. A cache-backed roster returns 88 people and LOOKS complete. The live walk returns 398, matching both an independent raw `users.list` walk and the separately-built `handles` map. Two code paths, one number. Cost is 7 requests of a 20/min tier on a human-invoked verb, which is why the decoder reads the cache instead.

## Evidence

Every acceptance criterion executed live and recorded in the design doc next to the criterion it proves. Full matrix in `docs/shakedown-slack-directory.md`.

- `read --resolve-mentions` over 200 messages of `#eng-on-call`: 135 usergroup mentions resolved, 0 raw, 0 encoded spans surviving, 22 lines of HTML entities cleaned. Rendered line count identical with and without the flag, so nothing was dropped.
- `search --mentions @mbp-oncall`: 34 survivors of 100 candidates. All 34 carry the entity. All 34 have raw text that never spells the handle. 0 of the 17 word-only hits from a plain text search survive.
- `slack users`: 398 == independent walk == `handles` map, > 88 (the cache map), > 200 (pagination completed).
- `channels members`: `#eng-baop` 31 == `num_members` 31. `#eng-on-call` 93 == 93.

## Five doc claims corrected against measurement

The design doc asserted each of these as fact. Live traffic disagreed.

1. The Slack token gained the scope IN PLACE. No re-mint, so nobody has to clear their token cache.
2. `user_count` arrives as a bare number, not a quoted string. Right conclusion (tolerant deserializer), inverted premise.
3. `previous_names` is MOST RECENT first, not oldest first.
4. A criterion invoked `slack write --print -m`. `-m` is not a flag `write` has, and `--print` skips mention resolution by design. It named the one flag that routes around the code path it was written to test.
5. `conversations.info` omits `num_members` unless `include_num_members=true` is sent. That criterion was sound and the code was not, so I fixed the code rather than softening the criterion.

## Implementation audit

Review panel, Mode 2. Six findings: five fixed, one doc-corrected.

Worth flagging for anyone reading the panel output: the Architect (Gemini) returned zero findings and a READY verdict while two of its explicit "verified" claims were checkable and wrong. The Staff Engineer (Codex) carried the pass. A clean bill from one reviewer is not a panel result.

Sharpest finding: Phase 2's acceptance criterion had NO failing test. Proven by breaking the code (summary hard-wired to 0 usergroups and no watermark, so storage still runs and only reporting drops) and watching the old test stay green. It bites now.

## Known gaps, documented not fixed

- 32 of 32 channel mentions in a 200-message read render raw. `users.conversations` only indexes channels you are a member of, so a cross-channel pointer cannot resolve. Raw is the designed rendering for an unresolvable id.
- `--mentions` combined with free text returns nothing: Slack stops treating `@handle` as a mention operator once a text term is present. `@mbp-oncall` alone is 218 candidates, `@mbp-oncall ticket` is 57201, the same total `ticket` returns alone. Narrow with `--in` or a date bound instead. In the flag help, the skill, and the README.
- The four prose enumerations across `README.md` and `plugin/README.md` are still hand-maintained and un-guarded. `plugin-guard` compares verbs to skill directories and never reads prose.

## Release

`0.2.9 -> 0.3.0`. Minor: three new verbs and two new flags, all additive, no breaking changes. Bump rides this PR, tag after merge.

Turn an opaque S… id into a readable @handle, find a group by name, and list
the groups a person belongs to. usergroups.list is un-paginated, so every
query is one call; the filters (query, --user, --empty, --include-disabled)
compose client-side over the full listing.

The verb, its skill, and its MCP tool ship together because plugin-guard
enforces CLI-verb <-> skill lockstep both ways.

Notable choices, all reasoned in the implementation notes:

- JSON emits a projected GroupJson, not the wire UserGroup. Serializing the
  wire struct would ship user_count while the text printed member_count(),
  which prefers users.len() -- two names for one concept, free to disagree
  the moment --members is passed.
- --empty excludes an UNKNOWN count rather than treating it as zero, and
  --user on an unknown handle is a loud error, not an empty list. A typo'd
  handle must not read as "this person is in no groups".
- The unresolved-mention message now splits PERSON from USERGROUP. The old
  single sentence told everyone to "disambiguate with an explicit id

the part actually worth your time: comparing marquee against persona-mcp turned up a real spec bug in marquee.

• RFC 9728 s3 puts the PRM doc at `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp` when the resource id carries a path. persona-mcp had this right. marquee served it host-appended and 404'd its own canonical URL.
• Claude never noticed, because it follows the `resource_metadata` pointer in the 401 rather than constructing the URL from `resource`. so a spec violation sat in prod, invisible, because the one client we test with routes around it.
• fixed and shipped v1.17.2 -> https://github.com/tatari-tv/marquee/pull/81. verified live on both envs: canonical path 200, old path still 200 for compat, challenge pointer updated.

takeaway for SRE-3953: "Claude connects" is NOT a conformance test. we have 5 MCP servers on 2 different IdPs (marquee -> Okta, persona-mcp -> auth-svc) with no agreement on where discovery lives. a shared conformance check is worth doing regardless of which broker wins.

## Round 6, 2026-09-16: the implementation audit (Mode 2)

The first implementation audit this doc has had. Rounds 1 through 5 were all design reviews. Ordered by Scott, and it needed `PANEL_ROUNDS_ORDERED_BY_SCOTT=6` for a mechanical reason worth recording: `panel-round-guard.sh` derives mode from the doc's `Status:` line, so once the status changed from `Implemented` to `Partially implemented` a Mode 2 audit keys as a design-review round. A partially-implemented doc cannot get an audit without spending the design-review cap. That is a guard defect, not a policy, and it belongs to whichever chunk owns `panel-round-guard.sh`.

Scoped to Phases 0 through 7. Addendum A was explicitly out of scope. Verdict: **not clean.** 7 must-fix, 4 cheap wins, 4 defers, 8 of 8 questions answered. Wiring and registration were clean, all six registrations present and correctly matched, all five hook files resolving through the symlinks, and four of six acceptance criteria held.

**Five of the eight shipped rules carried a live deny-to-allow bypass, and four of them trace to one question the code never answered consistently: which copy of the command a predicate reads.** That is the same class as chunk B's single-quoted-verb hole, which this chunk fixed in its own Phase 1, reappearing in five new places.

Every must-fix was reproduced independently before folding. The fixes landed as `35e4d35` and `5156d60`.

- **M1. GH-WRITE allowed the attached long body form.** `--field=name=x`, `--raw-field=name=x`, `--input=p.json` all allowed while the separated form denied. `is_value_flag` / `is_body_flag` are exact-token tests, and `gh` accepts the attached spelling (verified live), so the call read as a bare GET. Fixed by splitting on the first `=` before testing.
- **M2. SECRET allowed a single-quoted credential path.** The artifact pre-filter gated on `$masked`, which has `mask_squote` applied, so the path was erased before the filter saw it and the whole branch was skipped. The branch below already read the heredoc/comment-masked copy; the `case` now reads the same one.
- **M3. Any slash-command turn authorized an arbitrary post.** `posting_intent` matched the literal word `message` inside the `<command-message>` wrapper tag. 58 of 400 sampled transcripts carry that tag and `/cli-shakedown` is one of the incident classes TARGET exists to catch, so this inverted the rule on its own founding case. Fixed by stripping markup before matching, keeping inner text so `<command-args>send this to russ</command-args>` still counts. The existing slash-command fixture used `<command-name>` only, which is why the matrix never saw it.
- **M4. SLACK judged only the first posting statement.** The statement loop `break`s, and everything downstream is built from one statement's variables, so `slack write scott.idler aaa; slack write engineering bbb` was authorized by the exempt first target. Evaluating every statement properly means restructuring the whole downstream path, so the shape is refused instead: two posting statements in one command deny and the text says to split them. This is also the 2026-06-09 duplicate class. The narrowing is deliberate and Phase 9's replay will surface any legitimate compound post.
- **M5. PUBLIC-REPO ignored extra refspecs and the bulk forms.** The push read `sed -n '2p'`, so `git push origin main dirty` walked only `main`, and `--all` / `--mirror` carry no refspec at all and were never walked. Both are named in the doc's own "cases to model" list. Now every source is walked.
- **M6. INGEST's door was command-wide.** One `BULK_INGEST_ORDERED_BY_SCOTT=1` statement short-circuited the entire deny block, so every later ingest in the same command was laundered. The spec already said the opposite: count <= n allows the STATEMENT. The door now removes only its own statement from scope.
- **M7. `intent-guard.sh` failed OPEN on an unreadable `lib.sh`.** It carries PUBLIC-REPO, which the implementation contract names as fail-closed. `slack-post-guard.sh:182` had it right; this hook shipped the tree's older fail-open line.

Cheap wins, all folded:

- **C1** `cd -- <dir>` defeated the LN cwd tracker, because any operand starting with `-` was dropped. `--` is the end-of-options marker, not an option.
- **C2** No blob-size check on the commit path, while the shared deny text advertises one and the rule head names `git commit`. On commit the bytes are still in the working tree, so size is measured there.
- **C3** The heredoc extractor entered body state only for a `.sh` target, so it kept scanning THROUGH a `.md` body and re-armed on any line inside ending in `.sh` before a `<<`. Measured on the real artifact: writing this design doc through a quoted heredoc made the old extractor emit 1145 lines and deny. Two states now, and the comment that claimed the opposite is corrected.
- **C4** INGEST counted ops on the unquoted copy while the clauses read the masked one, so quoted prose denied. This fired on three of the audit's own commands, including its first attempt to write its probe file, and on two of this session's.

C3 and C4 compound into the exact false-positive class `lib.sh` exists to kill, reappearing in the one rule that deliberately opted out of statement scoping. That is the lesson to carry: an opt-out of the shared parser is an opt-in to re-deriving its bug list.

Recorded, not fixed, with the reason:

- **D1** `gh api repos/o/r/ -X PATCH` allows on a trailing slash, because the glob matches an empty third segment. GitHub 404s that route, verified, so the call cannot write. Predicate brittleness, not a bypass. The architect called it a silent bypass and that is overstated.
- **D3** `slack scheduled deliver` is unguarded; the subcommand matcher is `write|repost`. It drains a queue of follow-ups whose parent `slack write --at` was already checked, so no unchecked body enters.
- **D4** `cur_cwd` is the post-command cwd, so a trailing `cd` moves the repo PUBLIC-REPO audits. The audit could not construct a case that behaved differently from M5.
- **New, found while fixing C3 and out of this chunk's scope:** `lib.sh`'s `mask_heredoc` does not mask heredoc bodies on these inputs at all, which is why body text reaches `verbscan` in the first place. This chunk stopped editing `lib.sh` after round 2 measured an obvious fix there flipping two shipped guards from allow to deny, so it is handed on rather than touched.

Two mutations the audit ran proved the suites were blind to M2 and M4: reverting each fix left its suite at the pre-existing pass count. 16 fixtures were added across the three suites, each one verified to FAIL against the shipped code and pass against the fix. intent 167 -> 183, secret 189 -> 192, slack 123 -> 129.

On the seats: the architect returned rc=0; the staff seat was killed by the 10-minute timeout while composing its report, rc=124, no report produced. Its 737 KB trace was mined for leads and every lead was re-tested independently, with two claims dropped for not reproducing. The panel agent's own report was therefore its synthesis plus its own verification, which is why every finding above carries a probe rather than a citation.

## Standing after six rounds

The pattern is six for six: **every round has found at least one rule whose stated mechanism could not perform its stated job.** Round 1 `realpath -m`. Round 2 a ledger nothing could write. Round 3 a lock that did not span the operation. Round 4 a skip list that did not cover the flag it had just fixed. Round 5 a guard whose recipient loop the rule never reaches and a cache fill no process on the post path runs. Round 6, five predicates reading the wrong copy of the command.

The design-review question that catches this class is "what process, at what moment, runs this, and what can it see?" Round 6 adds the implementation-time sibling, and it is the sharper one for a guard: **which COPY of the command does this predicate read, and does every clause in the rule read the same one?** Five of the seven must-fixes are that question unanswered. It belongs in the implementation contract, not in a review.

TAIL = '''def walk():
    """Every Slack write in the live projects tree, as a replayable payload.

    This is the half that drifts. Measured on one afternoon during review: 236
    posts, then 237, then 239, then 240. So a count taken here has moved by the
    time Phase 3 runs, which is a cross-repo ship later. Phase 3 replays a
    snapshot of this instead of calling it.
    """
    posts = []
    for path in ROOT.rglob("*.jsonl"):
        try:
            raw = path.read_text(errors="replace").splitlines()
        except Exception:
            continue
        if not any('"mcp__slack__chat_' in l or "slack write" in l for l in raw):
            continue
        records = []
        for line in raw:
            try:
                records.append(json.loads(line))
            except Exception:
                records.append({})
        for i, rec in enumerate(records):
            if rec.get("type") != "assistant":
                continue
            for block in (rec.get("message") or {}).get("content") or []:
                if not isinstance(block, dict) or block.get("type") != "tool_use":
                    continue
                name = block.get("name")
                inp = block.get("input") or {}
                if name in WRITE_TOOLS:
                    kind, tool_input = "mcp", inp
                elif name == "Bash" and "slack write" in (inp.get("command") or ""):
                    kind, tool_input = "bash", inp
                else:
                    continue
                posts.append({
                    "kind": kind,
                    "tool_name": name,
                    # Stored VERBATIM and untruncated. The scored rows clip target
                    # to 60 and text to 90 for reading, so they are a summary and
                    # can never be replayed: the guard would see a different body.
                    "tool_input": tool_input,
                    "window": typed_prompt(records, i),
                    "cwd": str(pathlib.Path.home()),
                    "session": path.name,
                })
    # rglob order is filesystem order, so a re-walk reshuffles. The counts do not
    # care, but 0a's gate is that the file replays to the SAME counts twice and a
    # stable order makes the scored rows byte-comparable too.
    posts.sort(key=lambda q: (q["session"], q["tool_name"],
                              json.dumps(q["tool_input"], sort_keys=True)))
    return posts


def score(posts, guard):
    """Ask `guard` about every post. Returns the summary rows."""
    rows = []
    tmp = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    for post in posts:
        window = post["window"]
        txf = tmp / "tx.jsonl"
        txf.write_text("".join(
            json.dumps({
                "type": "user", "isSidechain": False,
                "promptId": "P1" if k == len(window) - 1 else f"P{k}",
                "promptSource": "typed",
                "message": {"content": c},
            }) + "\\n" for k, c in enumerate(window)))
        payload = {
            "hook_event_name": "PreToolUse",
            "tool_name": post["tool_name"],
            "tool_input": post["tool_input"],
            "transcript_path": str(txf),
            "prompt_id": "P1",
            "cwd": post["cwd"],
        }
        tool_input = post["tool_input"]
        d, reason = verdict(payload, guard)
        rows.append({
            "kind": post["kind"],
            "tool": post["tool_name"],
            "target": tool_input.get("channel") or (tool_input.get("command") or "")[:60],
            "text": (tool_input.get("text") or tool_input.get("command") or "")[:90],
            "prompt": (window[-1] if window else "")[:90],
            "window": " || ".join(w[:60] for w in window),
            "decision": d,
            "rule": reason.split(":")[1].strip()[:44] if ":" in reason else reason[:44],
            "session": post["session"],
        })
    return rows


def deny_class(rule):
    """Which of the three deny families a rule string belongs to.

    Phase 3's decision rule scopes to TARGET alone. The multi-statement family
    postdates chunk D's baseline and is orthogonal to which TARGET variant
    ships; the artifact family is $S/$TMPDIR//tmp body-file paths that no longer
    resolve under a scratch HOME. Counting all non-artifact denies made the old
    criterion unsatisfiable by the SHIPPED guard: 17 against a bar of 9.
    """
    if rule.startswith("no typed turn in the last"):
        return "target"
    if rule.startswith("the body file"):
        return "artifact"
    if rule.startswith("this command carries"):
        return "multi-statement"
    return "other"


def report(rows):
    tally = Counter(r["decision"] for r in rows)
    classes = Counter(deny_class(r["rule"]) for r in rows if r["decision"] == "deny")
    print(f"posts={len(rows)}  allow={tally['allow']}  deny={tally['deny']}")

    for rule, n in Counter(r["rule"] for r in rows if r["decision"] == "deny").most_common():

                  f"md5={hashlib.md5(snap.read_bytes()).hexdigest()}")

    rows = score(posts, args.guard)
    pathlib.Path(args.out).write_text(json.dumps(rows, indent=1))

Chunk A: enforcement core (0d252b8..5faca7d, 15 commits)
- Sandbox + env config landed (the TMPDIR fix, allowlists, excludedCommands)
- prose.sh Stop/SubagentStop gate: blocks offer-closers, em-dashes, over-long asks
- emdash.sh PreToolUse deny at the tool boundary (Bash, edits, 11 MCP matchers)
- rails rewrites rm to rkvr rmrf unless the target is positionally regenerable
- rails denies compounds that smuggle a stage out of the sandbox
- Owned the handoff skill, added a resume mode; branch-slash rule

Chunk B: guard precision (473fb6d..96e6a79, 16 commits)
- lib.sh: shared quote-aware command parser; manifest, secret, and release guards all ported onto it
- branch-name-guard.sh + case-specific branch-pr-title-guard.sh denials
- git-release-guard gaps closed and its over-reach trimmed
- git -C cwd stripping in rewrite-cd-read.py; deleted git-no-dash-c
- hooks-preflight.sh + a CI resolve check, so registering a hook before its file exists fails loudly
- Its own round-1 audit caught the command-word anchor being a prefix regex: 22 deny verdicts had become allows

Chunk C: panel round cap (bff72f2..75b0b44, 13 commits)
- panel-round-guard.sh on the Agent dispatch, keyed (doc, mode), counter in ~/.cache
- review-panel.md 26,322 → ~21KB, lore and prompt bodies split to two files
- Poll snippet deleted from create-design-doc; rules/interaction.md points at the hook
- Every run-dir artifact suffixed -r$ROUND; Step 3's one-call mandate made executable again

Evidence, and it is uneven

Fired on real work in the window (firings / distinct sessions):
- rails compound-deny: 83 / 35, the strongest signal by far. It fired on my own cp && sed && otto mid-session.
- prose.sh offer-closer: 127 / 30, including twice on me today
- emdash.sh deny: 43 / 23
- secret-echo-guard: 38 firings
- manifest-scope-guard: 21 / 14
- branch-pr-title-guard: 15 / 7
- git-release-guard: 11 / 7
- branch-name-guard: 4 / 3
- block-question-picker: 3 / 2

Matrix-only, no independent live firing:
- panel-round-guard: 50 firings / 17 sessions, but nearly all of that is my own probing and my subagents' transcripts. The one genuine event is the audit dispatch: mode=2 rounds=1. It has never denied a real 4th round, because nobody has tried one yet.
- The lib.sh refactor is invisible by design. Its evidence is that the guards built on it fired, not a signal of its own.
- hooks-preflight: runs every session and every CI, always green. Zero-catch, so it has never proven it would catch anything outside its 8-case matrix.

Weakest link:
- The rm to rkvr rmrf rewrite: 3 firings, 1 session. Three times today I archived files by calling rkvr directly rather than letting the rewrite catch a plain rm, so I did not exercise it either. It is the highest-consequence rewrite in chunk A and the least proven in practice.

Backstop across all of it: 834 assertions in 11 matrices, all green, all running inside otto ci. Each of the three chunks also has break-the-code evidence on its own core comparison.

The caveat that matters

Two of the three chunks had their central mechanism broken after CI was green and after the acceptance criteria passed. B's command-word anchor was a prefix regex that turned 22 denies into allows. C's door could be opened by quoting the guarded document's own fenced example. Both were found by implementation audits, not by tests. So "834 assertions green" is the floor of confidence here, not the ceiling, and for panel-round-guard specifically the first real denial is still unobserved.

  sb borg ingest --file urls.txt                                          -> deny

`door_open` (intent-guard.sh:461) is command-scope and short-circuits the whole deny block

## [SYNTHESIS] Round 12

### The reframe that decides how to rank everything below

Both seats attacked the key's INJECTIVITY and both found failures. They are right that the key is
not injective. But injectivity was never achievable and is not the property that protects
correctness: the key deliberately drops a labeled link's URL, and item 8 forces that drop.

What actually protects correctness is the raw-block gate you added last round. On the LOCATOR
path, two candidates sharing a key are compared by raw blocks and any difference yields
`Failed("ambiguous … different bodies")`. So every collision both seats constructed degrades to a
loud failure, never a wrong parent. Their findings are real and their consequence is
fail-loud.

**With one exception, which is the blocker, and which neither seat found: reconcile has no such
gate.**

### Blocker: reconcile can silently adopt a different body. Mine.

Reconcile's rules are "only a non-lossy, UNIQUE match adopts" and "anything lossy or non-unique
goes to a human". Uniqueness is the only guard. There is no raw-block comparison anywhere in
reconcile.

So: a queued follow-up is `<https://a|docs>`. The thread contains one self-authored reply
`<https://b|docs>`, which the user posted through `slack write --thread`, so it carries the
signature. The URL is dropped from the key, so the two match. The match is UNIQUE, exactly one
reply for exactly one follow-up. Reconcile adopts it, sets `delivered_ts`, and posts nothing. The
real follow-up never appears, silently.

The doc's own sentence two lines below condemns this: "a duplicate post and a silently skipped
post are both worse than a human looking". Round 11 fixed exactly this defect class in the
locator and left the sibling path untouched.

**Fix: apply the same gate. Before adopting, compare the reply's raw `blocks` against the
follow-up's. For a follow-up the queue has no stored blocks for, that comparison is unavailable,
so adoption should require the key match AND either stored blocks that agree or a lossy-free
whole-body equality; anything else is `failed: reconcile ambiguous`.** The conservative version is
simply: if the only evidence is a key match and the key is known to drop the URL, do not adopt on
a link-bearing body, fail ambiguous.

### Q2: the seats contradict each other, and the architect is right

The architect constructed a separator collision. Staff brute-forced 2,621 generated shapes, found
none, and explicitly said "empty container plus non-empty neighbor keeps separate prefixes".

I adjudicated against the doc's exact rules (lines 255-262). The architect is right:

```
tree A   rich_text > rich_text_list > rich_text_section("A")
         \u{2}r  \u{2}l  \u{2}s  t1:Ay0:

tree B   rich_text > [ rich_text_list (empty) , rich_text_section("A") ]
         \u{2}r  \u{2}l  \u{2}s  t1:Ay0:
```

Identical strings. The doc's own two rules produce it: `rich_text_list` emits `\u{2}l` then each
child section with its own `\u{2}s`, and "An empty container emits its separator and nothing
else". A prefix-only scheme cannot distinguish descending into a child from moving to a sibling.
Staff's generator evidently did not include an empty list adjacent to a section; its negative
result is not admissible against a construction that checks out by hand.

Consequence today: loud ambiguity via the locator gate, not a wrong parent. Reachability is low,
since this CLI's converter emits bullets as plain sections and never a list (item 9), so it
matters mainly for hand-typed replies in reconcile, which is where the gate is missing. Fix is one
byte: emit a terminator after a container's children, or a child count in the prefix.

### Q4: "one identity loss" is false. Both seats, and they found different items.

Combining both lists, the key drops all of these, not one:

| dropped | line |
|---|---|
| a labeled link's URL | 300-304, the only one currently owned |
| container attributes: `contains_padding`, `style`, `indent`, `border` | 262 |
| a `date` element's timestamp and format, keeping only `fallback` | 275 |
| a standard emoji's `name` when `unicode` is present | 271-273 |
| link styling, which Phase 1 explicitly expects to key identically | 897 |
| text style false-versus-absent, since only true flags are kept | 267-268 |

Two different `date` elements pointing at different timestamps but sharing a fallback string
collide. A nested list and a flat one collide via `indent`. All fail loud on the locator path and
all are unowned in prose.

### Q5: two more unverified absolutes, staff's, both fair

- **"candidates are all fired messages under the same parse rules"** (lines 347-349) is the
  argument that makes the raw-block gate sound, and it overstates. A candidate can be a LIVE
  self-authored message, not only a scheduled-fired one, and live-versus-scheduled raw block
  parity was never measured. The gate still fails safe if they differ, but the justification
  should say "all retrieved from history" rather than claiming parse-rule identity that no probe
  established.
- **"every message this CLI posts gets `blocks` from Slack (items 1, 8)"** (line 332). I checked:
  `PostResult` carries only `channel` and `ts` (`src/slack/api.rs:535-538`), and items 1 and 8

  for messages read back from history, but it is not what those items measured.

The architect adds a third: `normalize_text` renders multi-scalar emoji as hyphen-joined lowercase
hex "the same token shape `block_key` emits from Slack's `unicode` field", but item 8 measured

variation selector is unmeasured. This affects the TEXT FALLBACK only, where a mismatch produces
no match rather than a wrong match, so it fails loud. Worth a hedge in the text or a small probe,

### Q1 and Q3 clear

**Cheap-win (2)**
5. Hedge or probe the multi-scalar emoji `unicode` format used by the text fallback.
6. Correct the line 332 claim about live posts and `blocks`.

### Answers to the six questions

- **Q1** answered. Both seats: the gate is correct for its purpose. No concrete false negative

- **Q2** answered, seats contradict. The architect's collision is real and I verified it by hand;

- **Q4** answered. Both seats: false. Six drops, listed above.
- **Q5** answered. Three surviving absolutes, all fair.
- **Q6** answered. Not ready to build, on one blocker neither seat found: reconcile's missing

## [SYNTHESIS] Round 2

### Seat behavior this round

Both seats improved on round 1. The architect answered the six numbered questions AND the six
general review items this round (it skipped the general items in round 1). Staff cited file and
line for nearly every claim. Neither seat ran `cargo test` or `otto ci`; neither did I. Every
CI statement below is `[SOURCE-VERIFIED, NOT RUN]`.

### New must-fix findings

**M1. `deliver` holds the queue lock across all its network I/O, and `write --at` blocks on it.**
(architect; verified by me.) Doc lines 224-231: "`deliver` takes an exclusive advisory lock on
`<queue>.lock` **for its whole run**" and "`write --at` and `cancel` take **the same lock** for
their read-modify-write". `deliver`'s run contains `auth.test`, `chat.scheduledMessages.list`,
a paged `conversations.history`, and N `chat.postMessage` calls. So an interactive
`slack write --at` fired while the minutely timer is delivering blocks for as long as those
calls take.
Verified this text is **unchanged since round 1** (r1 snapshot line 207 carries the same
sentence), so this is a genuine new catch on old text, not a regression introduced by the
round-1 fixes. Neither seat found it in round 1.
Fix, per the architect: split the two locks. A `deliver.lock` held for the whole run enforces
the singleton. The queue file's own lock is taken only around each read-modify-write, including
each `delivered_ts` persist. That preserves both invariants (no double post, no lost append)
without serializing the CLI behind network I/O.

**M2. The new jitter band can thread follow-ups under the wrong message.**
(staff; verified by me at doc lines 185-187.) Step 2 reads: candidates with `ts` in
`[post_at - 2, post_at + 2]`, "exactly one -> `Found(ts)`". There is **no text check on that
path**. A single unrelated self-authored, top-level, plain message at `post_at - 1.5` satisfies
step 1 and step 2 and wins, and the real parent has not even fired yet.
This is a defect **introduced by the C1 fix**. Round 1's narrow step was `floor(ts) == post_at`,
a 1-second window entirely at or after `post_at`. The band is 4 seconds wide and half of it
sits BEFORE `post_at`, which is the region the doc's own Risks row labels "Unmeasured (0/2)".
The fix widened the false-positive surface fourfold and extended it into the region where the
true parent has never been observed.
Worse, **Phase 1's test suite pins the bug rather than catching it.** The criteria at doc lines
578-585 include "one at `post_at - 1.5` -> `Found` (early fire inside jitter)" and no negative
case at all for a band candidate whose text does not match.
Fix: require a normalized-text match for any candidate at `ts < post_at`, and add staff's
negative test (one self-authored band candidate, mismatched text, expect `Waiting`, not
`Found`).

**M3. A transient error inside the set loop becomes terminal.**
(architect.) The doc says `deliver` "never `?`s out of the loop on a set's API error" and that
a Slack error on one set is "written to that set's `failure`". `failure` is now TERMINAL. The
doc names only `not_in_channel` and `channel_not_found`, both correctly terminal, and separately
covers "a transport-level failure **before any set is touched**". It never says what happens to
a `ratelimited` or 5xx that hits `chat.postMessage` on set 3 of 5. Read literally, that set is
marked terminally failed and needs a human to run `--retry-failed`.
Fix: classify per-set errors. Terminal set writes `failure`; transient leaves the set untouched
for the next tick, the same shape as `Waiting`.

### Divergence: Q1 exit code. The seats split, and this is Scott's call.

- **Architect: exit 1 for as long as ANY set is in a failed state.** A `Type=oneshot` unit
  clears its failed state the moment a later run returns 0. With a minutely timer, "loud once"
  is visible to `systemctl --user --failed` for at most 60 seconds and then vanishes. That is
  not an operator signal.
- **Staff: keep exit-1-once.** It avoids a permanently failed unit while still marking the
  transition, and staff's separate point is that the doc should not oversell "loud once" as
  durable systemd state.

Both seats agree on the underlying systemd fact. They disagree only on what to do about it.

**My recommendation: the architect's. Exit 1 whenever any set is terminal-failed.**
Three reasons, and one clarification.
1. **This does not reopen the round-1 objection.** The architect's round-1 complaint reads like
   a reversal, but it is not. Round 1 objected to infinite RETRY plus exit 1: the cost was a
   network call per set per minute forever. The round-2 design already removed the retry, so a
   terminal set now costs zero network calls per tick. The exit code and the retry policy are
   separable, and only the retry was ever the problem.
2. **A persistently failed unit does not stop delivery.** systemd timers trigger their unit
   regardless of the previous run's result, so other queued sets keep delivering normally.
3. **It matches the owner's standard.** `~/repos/.claude/rules/taste.md:87` reads "Fail loudly,
   fail closed." A signal that self-erases after 60 seconds is not loud.

Clarification either way: staff is right that the doc must say precisely what the operator sees.
State that `systemctl --user --failed` is the durable signal, or state that it is not and the
journal line plus `slack scheduled list` are.

### Q6 follows Q1

Architect says the operator signal is insufficient without `OnFailure=`; staff says no

## [SYNTHESIS] Round 4

### The panel was wrong in round 1, and the measurement corrects it

Round 1 recommended cutting long-body chunking. I sided with the architect on the premise that
"a single on-time wall of text is practically superior to a fragmented thread." Nobody had
measured the fired result. Phase 0 item 6 (doc lines 61-67) measures it and the premise is
false: a 9000-char scheduled body fires as three top-level messages, and a 41,000-char body
fires as four, losing 25,000 characters silently. There is no wall.

**Both seats reverse position, explicitly and with no concrete flaw.** That is the strongest
convergence this panel has produced across four rounds. The reversal is correct and the doc
records it properly.

The coupling neither seat named: chunking is now **required** by the round-3 locator, not merely
preferable. The locator demands that stored `parent_text` equal what Slack holds. An unchunked
9000-char body is held by Slack as three fragments, none of which equals the stored 9000-char
text, so the locator could never find the parent. Chunking and the text-required locator are one
decision, and cutting the chunking goal would break the locator on every long body.

### Must-fix

**M1. The emoji-drop rule creates a wrong-parent false positive. BOTH SEATS, same
counterexample, constructed independently.**

Doc line 224 claims dropping emoji "cannot create a false positive on its own". Both seats
falsified it with the same structure. Staff's version: the scheduled parent is `deploy ✅` and
fires at `post_at + 3`; the same user has `deploy ❌` at `post_at + 1`. After dropping emoji both
project to `deploy`, giving two text matches. Step 4 then prefers the candidate inside
`[post_at - 2, post_at + 2]`, which is the **wrong** message, because the real parent fired
outside the band but inside the 600s window.
This is a defect this round introduced, and it defeats the round-2 fix that made text mandatory
precisely to prevent wrong-parent delivery.
Staff's fix is the right one and is fail-closed: if normalization dropped emoji **and** more than
one text match remains, return `Failed("ambiguous")` rather than resolving by jitter. The
architect's alternative, a unicode-to-shortcode lookup table, is strictly more work for the same
outcome and adds a table that must track Slack's emoji set.

**M2. `\p{Extended_Pictographic}` does not cover the modifiers, so emoji do not actually cancel
out. Mine, measured.**

Staff raised this by reasoning (variation selectors, ZWJ, skin tones). I verified it against the
exact table the implementation would use. `EXTENDED_PICTOGRAPHIC` in
`regex-syntax-0.8.11/src/unicode_tables/property_bool.rs`, 71 ranges:

| scalar | Extended_Pictographic |
|---|---|
| ZWJ U+200D | false |
| VS16 U+FE0F | false |
| skin tone U+1F3FB | false |
| grinning U+1F600 | true |
| red heart U+2764 | true |

So a sent `❤️` (U+2764 U+FE0F) loses the heart and **keeps U+FE0F**. A sent `👍🏽` keeps the skin
tone modifier. A ZWJ family sequence keeps two ZWJs. The Slack side is a `:shortcode:` and drops
completely via the shortcode pattern. The two sides therefore do NOT project to the same string,
and the result is a hard no-match, which is exactly the never-found failure round 3's M1 existed
to close.
Fix: extend the class to `[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\u{FE0F}\u{200D}\u{1F3FB}-\u{1F3FF}]`, or
drop by grapheme cluster.
Separately I confirmed the doc's parenthetical is TRUE: `Extended_Pictographic` is present in
regex-syntax's `property_bool.rs`, and `fancy-regex = "0.18.0"` (`Cargo.toml:23`) carries default
features, so the class is available. That claim needed checking and it holds.

**M3. "Strictly better than today" is not honest. BOTH SEATS, same arithmetic.**

The Risks row at doc line 986 says chunked-top-level is "strictly better than today". Phase 5
makes installing the timer a manual operator step (doc line 977). With no timer:
- today: 16,000 chars land on time as top-level fragments;
- chunked: 4,000 chars land on time and the tail sits in `follow-ups.json` indefinitely.

4,000 delivered is worse than 16,000 delivered. Staff's replacement wording is the honest one:
"Better under the documented operating model where `scheduled deliver` runs; without a running
deliverer, long-body overflow remains queued locally until manual or timer delivery." Keep the
`desk.lan` mitigation, drop "strictly better".

**M4. `for_each_span` cannot implement the projection the doc specifies. Staff only, verified.**

Doc lines 210-213 specify the projection as running "through the existing `decode::for_each_span`
+ `classify`". Verified against the code, that recipe does not work:
- `for_each_span(input, f)` (`src/slack/decode.rs:316`) hands the callback only a `Span<'_>`. It
  yields no byte ranges and never yields the text BETWEEN spans, so the projected string cannot
  be rebuilt from it. You would get the spans and lose all the prose.
- The range-preserving walker is `substitute` (`src/slack/decode.rs:396`), which appends
  `input[last..m.start()]` before each rendering. It is **private**, and it takes a
  `DecodeLookup`, which is a resolution dependency the projection must not have.

Phase 1 needs a new public projection helper in `decode.rs`, or a range-preserving span walker
exposed alongside `for_each_span`. This blocks the round-3 M1 fix from being implementable as
written. Worth keeping `for_each_span`'s `protect_code` step in whatever replaces it, so fenced
code is not span-scanned.

**M5. Stale Phase 0 text contradicts the new measurement. BOTH SEATS.**

Doc lines 672-675 still read "With a 41000-char body -> `ok:true`, echoed at 41000. Both
cancelled. So a long `--at` body is accepted and posts as one wall today". That is the
pre-measurement text and it directly contradicts item 6 at lines 61-67. Staff ran
`rg -n 'one wall|posts as one wall|fragment|truncat|strictly better'` and reports this as the only
surviving instance of the old premise.

### Cheap-wins

- **Q2.** Alternative 6 is correctly characterized, and "fallback, not the default" is the right

- **Q3 partially.** The projection is the right IDEA and closes round-3 M1 in intent for every

### Interaction with the five open round-3 must-fix items

Only one interacts. Round-3 M1 (a required text match makes real parents unfindable) is the item

### Round-4 ranked actions

**Must-fix (5)**

**Scott's call (1)**

### The one blocker, both seats, independently

**Slack's scheduled-list and history are not atomic, and the design treats them as if they are.**

Step 0 gates the locator on the id having LEFT `chat.scheduledMessages.list`. That proves "no
longer pending". It does not prove "visible in `conversations.history`". If there is any lag
between the two, the locator runs while the real parent is not yet visible, and a LOSSY decoy
sitting at `post_at - 1` satisfies the round-5 restriction (`post_at - 1` is not before
`post_at - 2`), is the only match, and is persisted as `parent_ts` forever, because the locator
never runs again for that set.

Both seats reached this independently and neither could find anything that forecloses it. Staff
checked Slack's published reference for both methods and reports they describe pending-message
listing and history retrieval but say nothing about cross-method visibility atomicity. The doc's
own evidence is two probes reading "same moment", which is an observation, not a guarantee.

The live file's "a lossy comparison never produces `Found`" removes this by construction. If that
wording survives, the blocker is closed. It needs to be reviewed, not assumed.

### The signature argument is unsound, both seats, and the code confirms it

Doc lines 313-316 argue a hand-typed reply cannot collide because the compared text carries the
attribution signature. Verified against the code, the argument does not hold:
- `sign` is `format!("{body}{signature}")` (`src/command/write.rs:1417`). No entropy, no nonce.
- The signature is a single global config value, `DEFAULT_WRITE_SIGNATURE` at `src/config.rs:23`,
  resolved into `Config.write_signature`. It is per-installation, not per-message and not
  per-user.
- `slack write --thread <root>` posts through the same signed path, so a reply the same user
  sends through this CLI carries a byte-identical signature.

So the signature proves "written by this CLI with this config", never "this specific queued
follow-up already posted". The architect's sharpest version: a manual CLI reply that differs from
a queued follow-up ONLY by dropped emoji projects to the same string, is a unique lossy match,
and gets adopted, silently discarding the queued follow-up. The doc should claim only what the
signature actually establishes.

Staff adds a real edge I confirmed: `validate_write_signature` (`src/config.rs:342-350`) accepts a
signature consisting solely of `🤖` or `:robot_face:`. Under such a config the signature itself
projects away, so an emoji-only body really does normalize to the empty string and the round-5
B4 collision returns in full. The design must specify behavior on the SIGNED stored text, and
must not assume the signature survives projection.

### Reconcile's four rules hold

Both seats walked them and both cleared them, and I verified the anchors:
- Parent exclusion is correct and necessary: `conversations_replies`'s docstring states the parent

  filter, which `Message.user` supports (`src/slack/api.rs:173`).
- More than one candidate reply for one follow-up fails ambiguous.

The only residual is the lossy adoption path, which is the signature finding above, not a rule
defect.

## [SYNTHESIS]

### Seat tool limits (declare before reading findings)

- **staff-engineer (codex)** stated it did not run `cargo test` or `otto ci`: its sandbox is
  read-only and those write under `target/`. Its Phase-6 verdict is a **read of the test
  source**, not an execution.
- **architect (gemini)** answered only Q1..Q6. It produced **no answer to general review items
  (1)-(6)**: no independent risk list, no assumptions pass, no missing-decisions list, no
  acceptance-criteria audit, no unrequested-scope pass, no hardest question. That half of the
  architect seat is missing and I filled it below myself.
- **I did not run `otto ci` either.** Every "CI-green" statement below is source-verified by
  reading `src/surface/tests.rs`, not executed. Labeled `[SOURCE-VERIFIED, NOT RUN]`.

### Convergence (both seats, strongest signal)

**C1. The parent locator misses an early fire. MUST-FIX.**
Both seats independently landed on the same hole. The window is
`conversations_history_window(channel, post_at, post_at + 600)`. If the fired `ts` is even
fractionally below `post_at`, it is excluded by the `oldest` bound, and step 2 of the algorithm
(`floor(ts) == post_at`) misses it too. Two independent points break on the same event, and the
result is a 600s wait followed by a loud `failed` for a parent that posted fine.
Verified by me: `conversations_history` (`src/slack/api.rs:660`) takes only `oldest` - no
`latest`, no `inclusive`. The new `conversations_history_window` must send both explicitly;
`conversations_history_at` (`src/slack/api.rs:718-724`) is the in-repo pattern.
Fix: `oldest = post_at - EARLY_FIRE_SLACK_SECS` and widen the narrow step to a `ts` range rather
than exact floor equality.
`[UNVERIFIED]` caveat on the premise: **neither seat measured Slack firing early.** The doc's
own Phase 0 measured 2/2 firing 0.27s and 0.83s AFTER `post_at`. So this is defensive hardening
against an unmeasured case, not a reproduced bug. It stays must-fix because the fix is a single
constant and the failure mode is a loud false negative on the feature's main path.

**C2. Retrying a `failed` set forever is wrong. MUST-FIX. Answers Q3 against the author's lean.**
Architect: infinite retry combined with `deliver` exiting 1 on any failed set makes the systemd
unit fail every single minute, spamming the journal and tripping systemd failure handling.
Staff: the data model cannot support a stop even if you wanted one - `FollowUpSet` has
`failure: Option<String>` and nothing else. No `failure_count`, no `last_attempt_at`, no error
class, no backoff, no terminal state.
Both call for a terminal/abandoned state that returns the timer to a clean exit 0.
Architect adds a decision the doc never states: **`deliver` must not `?` out on one set's API
failure**, or one bad set starves every other queued set in the same run. The doc's per-set text
output implies per-set error capture but never says it.
Staff's related gap: the Risks table says a left channel yields "a loud `not_in_channel`", but
the doc never says whether that is persisted onto `failure` or merely errors on each tick.

**C3. Q1 `deliver`, not `flush`. Settled, agrees with the author.**
Both cite the literal-naming standard. Staff checked the repo for existing vocabulary with
`rg -n "flush" src plugin README.md` and found only composer internals
(`src/slack/compose.rs:84`). No reason to reopen.

**C4. Q4 the hybrid split is right. Settled, agrees with the author.**
Neither seat could name a concrete flaw. Both give the same reason: all-local makes the parent
itself depend on the machine being awake and the Okta session being healthy, which is the one
leg Slack does reliably. Staff adds a second cost the doc already names: a second parent id
space for `scheduled list` to merge.

### Divergence

**D1. Q2 keep or cut "a long `--at` body chunks into follow-ups". The seats split.**
- Architect says **CUT**. Phase 0 measured Slack accepting and posting a 41,000-char scheduled
  message with `ok:true` and no warning. Chunking converts one reliably-server-side post into a
  head chunk (server-side, on time) plus a tail held in the local queue. A sleeping machine then
  posts what looks like a truncated announcement at 9am with the rest arriving whenever the
  laptop wakes.
- Staff says **KEEP**, framed as contract repair rather than bonus scope. Verified: `README.md:113`
  states "A post over the practical size cap is never truncated - it threads on paragraph
  boundaries", and `run_schedule` (`src/command/write.rs:1189`) sends the whole signed body in one
  `chat.scheduleMessage` call at `:1205`, so `--at` violates it today.

**My read: the architect's objection is the stronger one, and the doc does not address it.**
Both facts are true and they are not in tension: the contract IS violated, and the proposed fix
DOES create a new failure mode. The Risks table has one row for "Machine asleep at `post_at`"
with Impact **Low**, mitigated by "Follow-ups post when it wakes". That is honest for
user-authored follow-ups, which are three discrete items. It is **not** honest when the
"follow-ups" are the back half of one continuous body. Same risk row, materially different
impact, and the doc never separates the two cases.
Recommendation: keep the goal only on the `--thread` path, where the chunks go server-side and
carry no local dependency, and cut it on the top-level `--at` path. If Scott wants it on both,
the Risks table needs a second row saying a split body can land half on time and half late.

**D2. Q6 line budget. Staff is wrong on the arithmetic; both are right on otto.**
Staff: "plausibly gets under 1250 only if `BroadcastReport::json` moves too" (`src/command/write.rs:343`).
I measured the actual spans. Moving exactly the doc's list:

### Findings neither seat raised

**N1. `unescape_entities` is private. CHEAP-WIN.**
`src/slack/decode.rs:488` declares it `fn unescape_entities`, not `pub`. Phase 1 puts
`normalize_text` in `src/slack/follow_ups.rs` and defines it as `unescape_entities` plus URL-angle
stripping. That is a cross-module call to a private item. Phase 1 needs a visibility bump to
`pub(crate)` (preferred - one definition of Slack's escaping rule) or it will silently duplicate
the function, and the decode.rs doc comment above it warns specifically that the ordering is
subtle and easy to get wrong.

**N2. `cancel` mid-delivery reports a count that can be a lie. CHEAP-WIN.**
`cancel` drops the local set and prints `cancelled Q… in C… (2 follow-ups dropped)`. If
`deliver` already posted follow-up 1 (its `delivered_ts` is set), one of those two is in Slack
and cannot be dropped. The text and `ScheduledCancelJson.follow_ups_dropped` should count only
follow-ups with no `delivered_ts`, and say so when some already posted.

**N3. No queue growth bound and no operator story for a failing timer. DEFER.**
Nothing caps `sets`, and with retry-forever a permanently-failed set lives in the file until a
human runs `cancel`. The unit file is `Type=oneshot` with no `OnFailure=` and no logging config,
so the doc never says what a persistently failing `deliver` looks like to an operator. This
folds into C2: fix the retry policy and this mostly resolves.

**N4. Clock skew on the failure deadline. DEFER.**
Local `now` drives the "failed after 600s" call. A fast local clock marks a set failed before
Slack has had the full window. Low impact: the set is retained and the next tick retries.

**New verb: `slack scheduled list|cancel`.** Mirrors the `channels members|info` shape already in the tree. `list` is always live (pending sends fire on their own schedule, so there's no local event to invalidate a cache against). `cancel` takes channel + id as positionals, matching `chat.deleteScheduledMessage`'s own required arguments.

**Two new Slack API wrappers** in `src/slack/api.rs`: `chat.scheduledMessages.list` and `chat.deleteScheduledMessage`, with their own test coverage in `src/slack/api/tests.rs`.

**Two new MCP tools**, `chat_scheduled_messages_list` and `chat_delete_scheduled_message`, landing right next to `chat_schedule_message` in the tool list (18 -> 20). went with a heartbeat line instead of a spinner. after N seconds with no output from a task, otto prints `[philo] still running (2m14s)` on stderr, once per interval. ordinary newline. no `\r`, no cursor control, no tty check deciding whether it shows up at all.

your log constraint picked the shape. a spinner cant clear it: the only way to not deface a log is to gate on is_terminal, and then it shows nothing in CI, under `2>&1 | tee`, or in a captured log, which is where "is it hung?" gets asked most.

slim-dump works for a specific reason. the drain reads `read_until('\n')`, so a `\r`-redrawn bar never yields a line, the idle clock never resets, and the task gets heartbeated. a tty-gated spinner shows you nothing on that exact case.

didnt merge #9. it redraws in place with `\r` + `\x1b[K`, which buys an erase-before-every-write invariant every current and future terminal writer has to honor, plus width truncation and cursor restore on SIGINT. comparison writeup is in the repo: `docs/design/2026-09-15-idle-indicator-comparison.md`

knobs: `--progress-interval <SECONDS>` | `OTTO_PROGRESS_INTERVAL` | `otto.progress-interval`. default 10, `0` disables.

fix(digest): starred + important only, and real Block Kit bullets

Three problems, all reported from the first live enriched digest.

The Needs Reply section should never have existed. The digest's own design doc
scopes it to "the mail currently pinned in the inbox (Starred and Important)"
and calls that set "the human's real action queue". The triage doc later bolted
on a section fed from llm/needs-reply, which inverted the product: the first
live run contributed 15 model-picked threads against the 5 actually pinned, 9
of them Greenhouse pipeline notifications ("X was moved into Hiring Manager
Review", "fill out your scorecard"), and buried the human's own picks at the
bottom. Pin is now Starred | Important, and the digest no longer queries the
bucket at all. Triage's labels and reply drafts still do their job in Gmail;
they just do not get to add rows here.

The bullets were not bullets. mrkdwn has NO list syntax, so the `  - ` prefix
rendered as a literal hyphen and the whole digest read as a text dump. Slack's
only real list is the Block Kit rich_text_list element, so digest/blocks.rs
emits one.

The escaping bug goes away by construction rather than by fix. escape_mrkdwn
converts < and > to entities, which is correct inside mrkdwn's <url|text> form,
but Slack does not decode them in link display text -- so a subject reading
"Mark <> Scott Sync" reached Slack as a visible "Mark <> Scott Sync".
Inside rich_text a text element's content is LITERAL and formatting comes from
a style object, so there is nothing to escape and no way to leak an entity.
Tests assert both the angle brackets and an ampersand survive intact.

Also fixes the split message: the digest arrived as TWO Slack messages cut
mid-thread, because BUDGET is 10000 while Slack splits chat.postMessage text at
4000. With blocks, text carries only a short notification fallback and the body
is not subject to that limit at all. Everything lands in ONE rich_text block
whose elements hold every line, because a message is capped at 50 blocks and
one-block-per-line would blow that at 20 threads.

Not yet wired to `slack write --blocks-file` (tatari-tv/slack-cli#43, merged but
untagged). Once that releases, the digest can drop its own hyper client,
digest.env, token-env and write_digest_env entirely: one authenticated CLI that
owns its own auth, the same shape as the keyless `claude` transport.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("plugin/skills/write/SKILL.md")
s = p.read_text()

s = s.replace(
    'argument-hint: "<#channel|permalink> <content...> [--file <path>] [--markdown-to-mrkdwn <path>]',
    'argument-hint: "<#channel|permalink> <content...> [--file <path>] [--markdown-to-mrkdwn <path>] [--blocks-file <path>]',
    1,
)

old = '''Use `--file` for binaries, PDFs, images, or any artifact the reader should
download; use `--markdown-to-mrkdwn` for prose you want rendered in-channel.'''
new = '''Use `--file` for binaries, PDFs, images, or any artifact the reader should
download; use `--markdown-to-mrkdwn` for prose you want rendered in-channel.

## Real bulleted and numbered lists: `--blocks-file`

**mrkdwn has no list syntax.** A `- item` line posts a literal hyphen, which is
why a converted Markdown list reads as a text dump rather than a list. Slack's
only actual list is the Block Kit `rich_text_list` element, and
`--blocks-file <path>` is how you send one.

```bash
slack write '#eng' --blocks-file ./digest.json
```

`<path>` holds a **JSON array of Block Kit blocks**. A bulleted list looks like
this; `"style": "ordered"` gives a numbered one instead.

```json
[
  {
    "type": "rich_text",
    "elements": [
      { "type": "rich_text_section",
        "elements": [{ "type": "text", "text": "Deploy summary\\n", "style": { "bold": true } }] },
      { "type": "rich_text_list", "style": "bullet",
        "elements": [
          { "type": "rich_text_section", "elements": [{ "type": "text", "text": "api rolled to v2.4" }] },
          { "type": "rich_text_section", "elements": [
              { "type": "text", "text": "see ", },
              { "type": "link", "url": "https://example.com/run/42", "text": "run 42" }
          ] }
        ] }
    ]
  }
]
```

Things worth knowing before you reach for it:

- **Text inside `rich_text` is literal.** Formatting comes from a `style`
  object, not from in-band markers, so `<`, `>` and `&` need no escaping and a
  subject like `Mark <> Scott Sync` survives intact. This is the opposite of
  the mrkdwn path, where those characters must be escaped.
- **The signature still applies**, appended as one additional `rich_text`
  block. It has to be a block: when a message carries `blocks`, Slack renders
  those and demotes `text` to notifications only, so a text-only signature
  would be invisible. There is no way to post unsigned.
- **No conversion, no mention resolution.** A `@handle` in a `rich_text` text
  element is literal. To ping someone, encode the id yourself as a `user`
  element, the same way `--raw` requires.
- **One message, never chunked.** The 4,000-character threading budget applies
  to `text`, and escaping that budget is a large part of why you would use
  blocks. Slack caps a message at 50 blocks, and the signature needs one, so
  prefer a *single* `rich_text` block with many `elements` over many blocks -
  one block's `elements` array has no such limit.
- Mutually exclusive with `--raw`, `--no-mentions`, `--file`,
  `--markdown-to-mrkdwn`, `--broadcast`, `--edit` and `--dm-mentioned`.

Reach for `--blocks-file` when a **program** is building the payload and needs
structure mrkdwn cannot express. For prose you are writing yourself, the normal
content path and `--markdown-to-mrkdwn` remain the right tools.'''
assert old in s, "skill anchor"
p.write_text(s.replace(old, new, 1))
print("SKILL.md documented")
PY
