🚨 *The Tech Spec process changed today.*

🔀 *So What Changed?*
• *Two templates instead of one*: with PRD | standalone. Standalone is for work that will never have a PRD, which is most Platform and Security work.
• *The database is retired.* No more Add New Entry. Every team page carries two buttons: click one and the page is created in your team space, already labelled, already carrying its header.
• *Approvals live on the Tech Spec itself*, in the Approvers row. Not in the Jira Epic.
• *There is no revision table.* The Status row carries it: Draft | In review | Approved | Superseded.

🔑 *So Why the Header?*
A Tech Spec with no header does not appear in the table on the index. It still exists, but only search will find it. That is the whole reason the header comes first. 248 of the 251 existing Tech Specs were backfilled this week, so the index finally lists the whole inventory!!!

📖 *So What Does It Mean for Me?*
<https://marquee.internal.tatari.dev/p/eng/tech-specs-what-changed/|Tech Specs: What Changed, and What It Means for You> walks the whole thing: what was wrong, how creating one works now, which template to pick, what went away, and what to check on the specs you already have.

🔗 *Where To Go*
• <https://tatari.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/1673199755/Engineering+Tech+Specs|Engineering Tech Specs> for the buttons and the full list
• <https://tatari.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/TPM1/pages/2476507199/Engineering+Tech+Spec+Process+Simple+Guide|Simple Guide> for the four phases and what goes in each header row
• <https://tatari.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/2680586322/Engineering+Tech+Specs+Legacy+Process+retired+2026-09-10|The old instructions> are kept for reference. *Do not follow them*: every create step in them now leads to the wrong template.

The point is that a Tech Spec should be findable by the people who need it, without knowing who wrote it or which space it landed in. Fill in the header and yours will be.

tool_input.text:
*The Tech Spec process changed today.*

*So What Changed?*
• Two templates instead of one: with PRD | standalone. Standalone is for work that will never have a PRD, which is most Platform and Security work.
• The database is retired. No more Add New Entry. Every team page carries two buttons: click one and the page is created in your team space, already labelled, already carrying its header.
• Approvals are recorded on the Tech Spec itself, in the Approvers row. Not in the Jira Epic.
• There is no revision table. The Status row carries it: Draft | In review | Approved | Superseded.

*So Why the Header?*
A Tech Spec with no header does not appear in the table on the index. It still exists, but only search will find it. That is the whole reason the header comes first. 248 of the 251 existing Tech Specs were backfilled this week, so the index finally lists the whole inventory!!!

*So What Does It Mean for Me?*
<https://marquee.internal.tatari.dev/p/eng/tech-specs-what-changed/|Tech Specs: What Changed, and What It Means for You> walks the whole thing: what was wrong, how creating one works now, which template to pick, what went away, and what to check on the specs you already have.

*Where To Go*
• <https://tatari.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/1673199755/Engineering+Tech+Specs|Engineering Tech Specs> for the buttons and the full list
• <https://tatari.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/TPM1/pages/2476507199/Engineering+Tech+Spec+Process+Simple+Guide|Simple Guide> for the four phases and what goes in each header row
• <https://tatari.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/2680586322/Engineering+Tech+Specs+Legacy+Process+retired+2026-09-10|The old instructions> are kept for reference. Do not follow them: every create step in them now leads to the wrong template.

The point is that a Tech Spec should be findable by the people who need it, without knowing who wrote it or which space it landed in. Fill in the header and yours will be.

If your Tech Spec is missing from the index, it just needs a header. Ping me and I will add it.

*Clyde 0.13.2 → 30-day usage report → Marquee → #ai-foundry*

*1. Update clyde to 0.13.2*
```
clyde update check                    # confirms 0.13.2 is available
clyde update install 0.13.2 --yes
clyde --version                       # should print: clyde v0.13.2
```
Building from source instead of the release binary:
```
cd ~/repos/tatari-tv/clyde
git fetch --tags && git checkout v0.13.2
./install.sh                          # cargo install --force --path clyde --bin clyde
```

*2. Collect the 30-day report*
`collect` fails if any session in the window isn't indexed yet, so reindex first:
```
clyde session reindex
clyde report collect --since 2026-06-24 -o ./claude-report.json
```
`--since` takes an absolute date, not a relative one — swap in today's date minus 30 days each time you run this. `--until` defaults to now.

*3. Render the report*
```
clyde report render -i ./claude-report.json --format html -o ./claude-report.html
```
(`html` is model-authored and needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set — no offline path for it.)

*4. Publish to marquee — use the `/marquee:publish` skill, not the CLI directly*
```
/marquee:publish ./claude-report.html
```
Skip `clyde report render --format marquee-html` for this step — that flag shells out straight to the `marquee` CLI itself. Rendering to local HTML and handing it to `/marquee:publish` keeps publishing on the approved skill path instead of clyde invoking the binary for you.

*5. Share it*
Post the URL `/marquee:publish` returns into #ai-foundry, with a one-line note on the report window (30 days, since date used).

---
*Don't have the `marquee` CLI/skill yet?*
It's distributed through the tatari-skills marketplace, not self-installed:
```
claude plugin marketplace add tatari-tv/tatari-skills
claude plugin install marquee@tatari-skills
```
This installs both the `publish-marquee` skill and the `marquee` CLI (pulled from marquee's GitHub releases) in one shot.

# Design Document: Scheduled follow-ups (thread replies under a scheduled parent)

**Author:** Scott Idler
**Date:** 2026-09-06
**Status:** Draft
**Review Passes Completed:** 1/5

## Summary

`slack write --at` schedules one message and stops. There is no way to say "and when it lands,
put these three items in its thread": Slack's own UI cannot do it (you cannot reply to a message
that does not exist yet), and neither can this CLI, for the same reason. `chat.scheduleMessage`
returns no `ts`, and a thread reply needs the parent's `ts`. This adds `write --follow-up <text>`
(repeatable): on a live post the follow-ups thread immediately; on a scheduled post they are held
in a local queue and `slack scheduled deliver` threads them once the parent has fired. `scheduled
list` and `scheduled cancel` learn about the queue so a pending set is never invisible or
orphaned. CLI + skill + MCP land together per `docs/design/2026-08-11-surface-lockstep.md`.

## Problem Statement

### Background

- Tatari's guidance page "Scheduling a Message in Slack" (Confluence, space SLK, page
  1423736835) tells people to schedule instead of posting at 11pm. Scott's note on it: "it does
  NOT let me post any follow up items, threaded under the initial message." The Slack client
  has no such control, and it cannot: a scheduled message has no `ts` until it posts.
- The CLI has the same ceiling. `write --at` (`src/command/write.rs:1189`, `run_schedule`)
  calls `chat.scheduleMessage` once and returns `{scheduled, scheduled_message_id, channel,
  post_at, thread_ts}`. `scheduled list|cancel` (`src/command/scheduled.rs`) inspects and
  cancels that one message. Nothing addresses "what happens after it fires".
- Live posts already thread. `post_chunks` (`src/command/write.rs:1130`) posts the first chunk
  as the parent and every overflow chunk under it, because the parent's `ts` comes back from
  `chat.postMessage`. The scheduled path cannot do this: `run_schedule` hands the whole signed
  body to `chat.scheduleMessage` unchunked (`:1197`), so the README's "a post over the practical
  size cap is never truncated - it threads" is false for `--at` today. It goes out as one wall.

### Root constraint, measured live (2026-09-06, `#clipboard` = `C0ANJQAJC7N`, every probe deleted)

1. **`chat.scheduleMessage` returns no `ts`.** Raw response: `{ok, scheduled_message_id:
   "Q0BVBJVQ526", channel, post_at, message: {user, type, bot_id, app_id, text, team,
   bot_profile, blocks}}`. No `ts` anywhere in `message`.
2. **A pending id is not a thread root.** `chat.scheduleMessage` with
   `thread_ts=Q0BVBJVQ526` -> `{ok:false, error:"internal_error", response_metadata:
   {messages:["[ERROR] 526000000 is not a valid thread_ts"]}}`. Slack tried to parse the `Q…` as
   a number. There is no server-side way to reply to a message that has not posted.
3. **The fired message's `ts` integer part equals `post_at`, twice out of two.**
   `post_at=1788712869` -> `ts=1788712869.266319`; `post_at=1788713080` ->
   `ts=1788713080.826989`. It appears in `conversations.history` with `user` = the caller
   (`U01G15A5EG6`) and drops out of `chat.scheduledMessages.list` at the same moment.
4. **Retrieved `text` is not what was sent.** Sent `a & b <c> "q" https://x.y/z?a=1&b=2`;
   history returns `a & b <c> "q" <https://x.y/z?a=1&b=2>`. Slack escapes `&<>`
   (already known: `src/slack/decode.rs:485`, `unescape_entities`) AND wraps a bare URL in
   `<…>`. Encoded spans `<@U…>`/`<#C…>` come back byte-identical. So an exact text match on
   the parent is not a reliable locator; `ts`-second equality is.
5. **A live `chat.postMessage` carries the same `bot_id`/`app_id`** (`B0BF87145HS` /
   `A0BF86XMRQC`, the Slack Valet app) as a fired scheduled message. Neither field
   distinguishes scheduled from live.

### Problem

**You cannot schedule a thread.** A human or agent writing an announcement at 11pm for 9am with
three follow-up items has two bad options: cram everything into one message, or wake up at 9am
and reply by hand. The second is what scheduling exists to remove.

The CLI is where this is fixable, because the CLI can remember. Slack will not hold a reply to
a message that does not exist; a local queue plus one verb that runs after `post_at` can.

### Goals

- `slack write --at <when> --follow-up <text> [--follow-up <text>…] <target> <parent>` schedules
  the parent through Slack and threads every follow-up under it after it fires, in order (Scott:
  "allow us to do that through our slack-cli").
- The same flag on a live post threads the follow-ups immediately (author: the flag means one
  thing regardless of `--at`; a caller should not need two vocabularies).
- `scheduled list` shows queued follow-ups and their state; `scheduled cancel` drops them with
  the parent (author: the lifecycle verbs must not lie about what is pending, per the
  scheduled-lifecycle design's "names tell the truth").
- Delivery is idempotent and resumable: a crash or a second concurrent runner never
  double-posts a follow-up (author: a duplicate reply in a public channel is the visible
  failure).
- A long `--at` body threads on fire the way a long live body threads now, by turning its
  overflow chunks into follow-ups (author: README `write` contract, currently violated by
  `--at`; same mechanism, zero extra moving parts).
- MCP: `chat_post_message` and `chat_schedule_message` take `follow_ups`; a `scheduled_deliver`
  tool exists; `chat_scheduled_messages_list` rows carry the queue state (lockstep rule).

### Non-Goals

- **Excluded: per-follow-up times** (`--follow-up-at`). Not asked for. Follow-ups post as soon
  as the parent is found. Parked, revisit if someone wants a drip.
- **Excluded: follow-ups on `--broadcast` copies.** Follow-ups thread under the primary only;
  crossposts get the pointer they get today. `--broadcast` + `--at` stays forbidden.
- **Excluded: follow-ups with `--file` / `--edit`.** Clap conflicts, same as `--at`.
- **Excluded: `--dm-mentioned` scanning follow-up bodies.** The fan-out DMs the parent's
  permalink and scans the parent body only. Parked; revisit if a follow-up needs to notify.
- **Excluded: a server-side runner (valet or a new service) holding the queue.** See
  Alternatives. Parked with a revisit condition: the queue must be delivered from a machine
  other than the one that scheduled it.
- **Excluded: the CLI installing its own timer** (`scheduled install-timer`). The unit files
  ship in-repo and the skill documents them; installing is an operator step. Parked.
- **Excluded: a queue that outlives one machine.** The queue is a local file; `list` shows the
  local queue. Documented, not hidden.
- **Excluded: editing a queued follow-up.** Cancel and reschedule, same as the parent.

## Proposed Solution

### Overview

```
slack write --follow-up A --follow-up B '#ch' 'parent'        (live)
  post parent -> ts
  post A under ts, post B under ts                             (post_chunks, thread_ts=ts)

slack write --at 9h --follow-up A --follow-up B '#ch' 'parent' (scheduled, top-level)
  chat.scheduleMessage(parent) -> Q…, post_at
  queue.append({id: Q…, channel, post_at, parent_text, follow_ups: [A, B]})
  -> prints the id + "2 follow-ups queued; deliver with `slack scheduled deliver`"

slack write --at 9h --thread <root> --follow-up A '#ch' 'parent' (scheduled, into a thread)
  chat.scheduleMessage(parent, thread_ts=root, post_at)
  chat.scheduleMessage(A, thread_ts=root, post_at+1)           (root is KNOWN: no queue)

slack scheduled deliver [--channel <ch>]
  for each queued set with post_at <= now:
    still in chat.scheduledMessages.list?   -> waiting, skip
    locate parent in conversations.history  -> ts | not-yet | failed
    post each undelivered follow-up under ts, persisting ts after EACH
    all delivered -> remove the set

slack scheduled list       rows gain FOLLOW_UPS: "-" | "2 queued" | "2 ready" | "1/2 delivered" | "failed: …"
slack scheduled cancel     cancels the Slack parent AND drops the local set
```

### Architecture

**Copy what exists.** Three shipped patterns cover every structural choice here:

- **`--broadcast` is the flag shape.** `Vec<String>` with `ArgAction::Append`
  (`src/cli.rs:246`), repeated never comma-split, documented "the greedy trailing content would
  swallow a space-separated list". `--follow-up` is declared identically, and the flags-before-
  positionals rule (`WriteArgs` message positional is `trailing_var_arg`) applies as it does to
  `--at`.
- **`post_chunks` is the delivery primitive.** It already posts a body under a `thread_ts`,
  chunks on overflow, and returns a typed `PartialPost` naming what did land
  (`src/command/write.rs:1076`). Each follow-up is one `post_chunks` call with the parent's
  `ts`; a follow-up over the cap threads its own chunks under the same parent.
- **`cache.rs` is the on-disk discipline.** Atomic temp-in-same-dir + `fsync` + `rename`, 0600,
  `IndexMap` for stable key order, no `deny_unknown_fields` so an old binary tolerates a newer
  file (`src/slack/cache.rs:30-33`, `:69-75`). The queue copies all of that. It does NOT copy
  last-writer-wins: see "Concurrency" below.

**The queue is state, not cache.** `~/.cache/slack/ids.json` can be deleted and rebuilt; the
queue cannot (deleting it loses messages). It lives under `XDG_STATE_HOME`
(`~/.local/state/slack/follow-ups.json`), config key `follow-ups-path`, resolved beside
`ids_cache_path` in `Config::resolve` (`src/config.rs:286`). `xdg_data_dir`/`xdg_cache_dir`
exist (`src/config.rs:54`, `:66`); `xdg_state_dir` is added next to them.

**Bodies are stored wire-ready.** Each follow-up is converted, mention-resolved and signed at
`write` time, and the queue stores that final text. `deliver` posts bytes; it never converts,
never resolves a mention, never signs. Reasons: the body a human reviewed is the body that
posts; a handle that gets renamed or deactivated between schedule and fire cannot change or
break the post; and `deliver` runs unattended, where a `mention-unresolved: fail` has nobody to
read it.

**Every follow-up is signed, individually.** The chunking rule ("the marker rides the final
chunk", `src/mcp/helpers.rs:212`) is about ONE body split for size. Follow-ups are distinct
posts a reader can land on from a permalink; each carries the attribution marker. The parent
carries its own.

**Locating the fired parent is `ts`-second first, text second.** From the measurements:

1. `auth.test` -> self user id (one call, already the pattern in `write`).
2. `conversations.history(channel, oldest=post_at, latest=post_at+1, inclusive)`, filter
   `user == self`. One hit -> that is the parent (this is the measured case, 2/2).
3. Zero hits -> Slack fired late or not yet. Widen to `latest=post_at+FIRE_WINDOW_SECS`
   (600), filter `user == self`, then keep the messages whose normalized text equals the
   normalized stored parent text (normalize = `unescape_entities` + strip `<…>` around a bare
   URL span with no `|`). One -> parent. Zero and `now < post_at + FIRE_WINDOW_SECS` ->
   `waiting`. Zero after the window -> `failed: parent not found`, set retained, exit non-zero.
4. More than one at any step -> normalized text match; still more than one -> `failed:
   ambiguous`, set retained.

A `failed` set is never silently dropped: `list` shows it with its reason, `cancel` removes it,
and re-running `deliver` re-attempts it (the parent may have appeared).

**Idempotent, resumable delivery.** After each successful `post_chunks`, the follow-up's
`delivered_ts` is written to disk BEFORE the next post starts. A crash mid-set resumes at the
first follow-up with no `delivered_ts`. A `PartialPost` from one follow-up's overflow is
recorded as `delivered_ts` = its parent-chunk ts plus `partial: true` and the set is marked
`failed: partial` so a human sees it; the remaining chunks are not retried automatically
(same policy as a live `PartialPost`).

**Concurrency: one deliverer at a time, by lock.** A systemd timer and an agent session can
both run `deliver` in the same minute. `cache.rs`'s documented last-writer-wins is fine for a
cache; here it means a double post. `deliver` takes an exclusive advisory lock on
`<queue>.lock` for its whole run (`flock(2)` via the `fs4` crate; std has no cross-process
lock). A second `deliver` that cannot get the lock prints `another deliver is running` and
exits 0: nothing to do, nothing wrong. `write --at` and `cancel` take the same lock for their
read-modify-write of the file, so an append cannot race a delete.

**Compensate, never half-schedule.** `write --at --follow-up` schedules the parent first
(Slack assigns the id), then appends to the queue. If the append fails (disk, permissions,
lock), the parent is cancelled with `chat.deleteScheduledMessage` and the command errors. The
alternative (queue first) leaves an id-less entry on a crash; this way the only possible
leftover is nothing.

**The `--thread` case needs no queue.** When the scheduled parent is itself a reply into an
existing thread (`--thread <root>` or a message-permalink target), the thread root is already
known, so each follow-up is scheduled through Slack with `thread_ts=root` and `post_at + i`
seconds (1-based) to keep order. Server-side, no local state, no `deliver`. Two mechanisms
behind one flag, chosen because the server-side one is strictly more reliable and is available
exactly when the root is known. Per-channel scheduling cap (~30 / 5 min, `RestrictedTooMany`)
applies; a refusal there cancels what was scheduled in this call and errors.

**Long `--at` bodies chunk into follow-ups.** `run_schedule` runs `compose::chunk` on the signed
parent. The head chunk is scheduled; each overflow chunk becomes a follow-up ahead of the
explicit `--follow-up` values. On the `--thread` path the same chunks go server-side. This is
the README contract, restored, with no new machinery.

**Line budgets.** `src/command/write.rs` is 1475/1500. The schedule path (`run_schedule`,
`ScheduleJson`, and the new follow-up code) moves to `src/command/write/schedule.rs` before any
behavior lands. `src/command/scheduled.rs` (323) absorbs `deliver` and the list/cancel changes.
`src/mcp.rs` (755), `src/mcp/helpers.rs` (814), `src/mcp/request.rs` (322), `src/surface.rs`
(1198) have room.

**No new Slack scope.** `conversations.history`, `chat.postMessage`, `chat.scheduleMessage`,
`chat.scheduledMessages.list`, `chat.deleteScheduledMessage`, `auth.test`: all already called.

### Data Model

`~/.local/state/slack/follow-ups.json`:

```rust
/// The on-disk queue of follow-up sets waiting on a scheduled parent.
#[derive(Debug, Default, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct FollowUpQueue {
    /// Keyed by scheduled_message_id. IndexMap for stable order across rewrites.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub sets: IndexMap<String, FollowUpSet>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct FollowUpSet {
    pub channel: String,
    pub post_at: i64,
    /// The parent body as SENT (signed wire text), for the text-match fallback.
    pub parent_text: String,
    pub created_at: i64,
    /// Set once the parent is located; the thread root every follow-up posts under.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub parent_ts: Option<String>,
    pub follow_ups: Vec<FollowUp>,
    /// `None` = pending/ready; `Some(reason)` = a human needs to look.
    #[serde(default)]
    pub failure: Option<String>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct FollowUp {
    /// Converted + mention-resolved + signed at `write` time. Posted verbatim.
    pub text: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub delivered_ts: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub partial: bool,
}
```

Derived, never stored: `state` for rendering is computed from the fields.

| state | condition |
|---|---|
| `queued` | `now < post_at` |
| `ready` | `now >= post_at`, `parent_ts` unset, `failure` unset |
| `delivering` | `parent_ts` set, some `delivered_ts` unset |
| `failed` | `failure` set |

A set with every `delivered_ts` set is removed from the file at the end of that `deliver` run;
there is no `done` state on disk.

Config (`slack.yml`, annotated in `slack.yml.example`):

```yaml
# Where `write --at --follow-up` keeps follow-ups until the parent fires. STATE, not cache:
# deleting it loses queued messages. Default: $XDG_STATE_HOME/slack/follow-ups.json.
# follow-ups-path: ~/.local/state/slack/follow-ups.json
```

Constants, in `src/slack/follow_ups.rs`:

```rust
/// How long after `post_at` we keep looking for the fired parent before calling the set failed.
/// Measured lag is under 1s (2/2); 600s is the loud-failure bound, not an expectation.
pub const FIRE_WINDOW_SECS: i64 = 600;
```

### API Design

CLI:

```
slack write [--at <when>] [--thread <ts>] --follow-up <text> [--follow-up <text>…] <target> <content>
slack scheduled deliver [--channel <#name|name|C…>]
slack scheduled list [--channel …]            # FOLLOW_UPS column added
slack scheduled cancel <CHANNEL> <ID>         # also drops the local set
```

`--follow-up` conflicts (clap) with `--edit`, `--file`, `--print` is allowed (renders parent then
each follow-up, separated by a `--- follow-up N ---` line), `--preview` is allowed (parent and
follow-ups go to the self-DM, threaded, since the ts is known). An empty `--follow-up ''` is a
typed error before any network call.

**Text output.**

`write` (live): the parent permalink, then one line per follow-up:
`follow-up 1/2 <permalink>`. Exit non-zero if any follow-up failed after the parent posted
(parent permalink still printed, same partial-failure policy as `--broadcast`).

`write --at` (top-level): today's line plus
`2 follow-ups queued; they post under the parent after it fires (slack scheduled deliver)`.

`write --at --thread`: today's line plus one `scheduled Q… follow-up 1/2 for <when>` per
follow-up.

`scheduled deliver`: one line per set touched:

```
delivered 2/2 follow-ups under https://tatari-tv.slack.com/archives/C…/p… (Q0BVBJVQ526)
waiting Q0BQGP1AHDF: parent has not fired (post_at 2026-09-13 15:00 UTC)
failed Q0BGM980XU1: parent not found within 600s of post_at
no follow-ups due
```

Exit 0 when nothing failed; exit 7 (generic) if any set is `failed`; `another deliver is
running` exits 0.

`scheduled list`: existing columns plus `FOLLOW_UPS`. A row for a set whose parent has already
fired (no Slack row) is rendered from the queue with the same columns. Empty everywhere still
prints `no scheduled messages`.

```
POST_AT           CHANNEL             ID           FOLLOW_UPS      TEXT
2026-09-07 09:00  #eng-oncall         Q0BQ8BQTGD9  2 queued        change freeze starts …
2026-09-06 15:00  #platform-internal  Q0BGM980XU1  failed: parent not found within 600s   deploy notes …
```

**JSON envelopes** (distinct per shape, per `src/command/write.rs:125-178`):

```rust

struct ScheduleJson { …existing…, follow_ups: Option<FollowUpsJson> }

// write (live), extended
struct WriteJson { …existing…, follow_ups: Vec<FollowUpPostedJson> }   // [] when none
struct FollowUpPostedJson { ts: String, permalink: String }

// scheduled list row, extended
struct ScheduledRowJson { …existing…, follow_ups: Option<FollowUpStateJson> }
struct FollowUpStateJson { count: usize, delivered: usize, state: String, failure: Option<String> }

// scheduled deliver
struct DeliverJson { sets: Vec<DeliverSetJson>, delivered: usize, waiting: usize, failed: usize }
struct DeliverSetJson { id: String, channel: String, state: String, parent_ts: Option<String>,
                        parent_permalink: Option<String>, delivered: usize, count: usize,
                        failure: Option<String> }

// scheduled cancel, extended
struct ScheduledCancelJson { cancelled: bool, id: String, channel: String, follow_ups_dropped: usize }
```

`cancel` semantics with a queue: drop the local set whether or not Slack accepts the cancel.
Exit 0 if either the Slack cancel succeeded or a set was dropped; exit 5
(`InvalidScheduledMessageId`) only when Slack refused AND there was no local set. Text:
`cancelled Q… in C… (2 follow-ups dropped)` or `Q… already posted or cancelled; 2 follow-ups
dropped`.

## Resolved Decisions

- **2026-09-06 (author): hybrid, not all-local.** The parent rides Slack's scheduler; only the
  follow-ups are local. An all-local runner would make the parent itself depend on a laptop
  being awake. See Alternatives 2.
- **2026-09-06 (author): `ts`-second locator, text as tiebreak.** Measured: retrieved text
  differs from sent text (entities, URL wrapping); `floor(ts) == post_at` held 2/2.
- **2026-09-06 (author): `--thread` follow-ups go server-side.** The root is known; no reason to
  hold them locally.

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: post the parent now, schedule the replies
- **Description:** `write` the parent live, then `write --at --thread <ts>` each follow-up.
  Works today with zero changes.
- **Pros:** No queue, no runner, all server-side.
- **Cons:** The parent posts now. That is the opposite of the ask.
- **Why not chosen:** Does not schedule the parent.

### Alternative 2: all-local scheduling
- **Description:** The queue holds the parent too; `deliver` posts the parent at `post_at` with
  `chat.postMessage` (gets the `ts` directly), then the follow-ups.
- **Pros:** No parent-location step, no text normalization, one mechanism.
- **Cons:** The parent no longer posts if the machine is asleep, offline, or the Okta session
  needs a human. Slack's scheduler has none of those failure modes. `scheduled list` would
  also have to merge two id spaces for the parent itself.
- **Why not chosen:** Trades the one reliable leg for symmetry. Recorded so it is not
  re-raised.

### Alternative 3: server-side runner (valet or a new service)
- **Description:** POST the follow-up set to a Tatari service that holds it and delivers it
  with the user's token.
- **Pros:** Delivers regardless of which machine scheduled; no timer to install.
- **Cons:** A new stateful service (or a valet feature) storing message bodies and acting on
  user tokens unattended; a cross-repo design; a bigger security surface than a local file.
- **Why not chosen:** Parked. Revisit condition: someone needs delivery from a machine other
  than the one that scheduled.

### Alternative 4: piggyback delivery on every `slack` invocation
- **Description:** Every `slack` command runs `deliver` first, so no timer is needed.
- **Pros:** Zero setup.
- **Cons:** `slack read` would post messages. A read verb with a write side effect is exactly
  the "two signals encode one meaning" class the taste rules forbid, and it is unpredictable
  (delivery happens when someone happens to run something).
- **Why not chosen:** Explicit verb, explicit timer.

### Alternative 5: a detached waiter spawned by `write --at`
- **Description:** `write --at` forks a background process that sleeps until `post_at` and
  delivers.
- **Pros:** No timer install.
- **Cons:** Dies on logout, reboot, sleep; invisible; racy with any other runner. Still needs
  the queue for recovery, at which point the timer is the simpler mechanism.
- **Why not chosen:** Strictly worse than queue + timer.

### Alternative 6: a `<ts>`-less text-only locator
- **Description:** Find the parent by exact text match in the channel after `post_at`.
- **Why not chosen:** Measured false: Slack rewrites `text` on retrieval (entities, `<url>`).
  Kept only as the normalized tiebreak.

## Technical Considerations

### Dependencies
- `fs4` (flock). One new crate; no new Slack scope; no new transport.
- Cross-repo: `tatari-tv/tatari-skills` pin bump after release (ship order: this repo first).

### Performance
- `deliver` with nothing due: 0 network calls. With one due set: `auth.test` + 1
  `chat.scheduledMessages.list` + 1-2 `conversations.history` + N `chat.postMessage`.
- Minutely timer cost is a file read.

### Security
- The queue holds message bodies (work-scoped content, may include private channel text) at
  0600 under the user's home, same posture as `~/.cache/slack/token.json`. Not a new class of
  data at rest for this tool.
- `deliver` posts only text that the same user composed and signed earlier; it cannot post
  anything it did not find in its own queue.
- Unattended runs use the existing silent-refresh Okta path; nothing new is stored.

### Testing Strategy
- Pure functions (`locate_parent`, `normalize_text`, `state`) get table tests.
- Every network path gets mockito call-count assertions (`.expect(n).assert()`), including the
  `expect(0)` negatives that prove no accidental call.
- The lock gets a two-thread contention test.
- Every test that guards a rule is broken once during implementation to prove it bites
  (implementation notes record which line was flipped).

### Rollout Plan
- Five phases, one commit each, `otto ci` green. Release after Phase 5. Timer installed on
  `desk.lan` by hand. Shakedown recorded.

## Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Slack fires late or `floor(ts) != post_at` under load | Low | Med | 600s window + normalized text fallback; failure is loud and retryable, never silent |
| Machine asleep at `post_at` | Med | Low | Follow-ups post when it wakes (`Persistent=true`); parent posted on time via Slack |
| Okta session needs a human on a timer run | Med | Low | Loud failure with the existing device-login hint; set retained; next tick retries |
| Two deliverers double-post | Low | High | `flock`; second runner exits 0 |
| Queue file lost | Low | Med | State dir, 0600, atomic writes; `list` shows what is queued so a loss is visible |
| Scheduled from laptop, timer on desktop | Med | Med | Documented per-machine scope; `list` is honest about being local; Alternative 3 is the revisit |
| Text normalization misses a Slack rewrite | Low | Low | Only a tiebreak; `ts`-second is primary; ambiguity fails loud |

## Open Questions

- [ ] `scheduled deliver` vs `scheduled flush` as the verb name. `deliver` says what happens to
      the messages; `flush` is the queue idiom. Author leans `deliver`.
- [ ] Should a `failed` set be retried automatically forever, or should `deliver` stop after N
      failures? Author leans forever (it is one history call per tick, and `cancel` is the
      off switch).

## Phase 5: SLACK

Commit: this phase. New hook `HOME/.claude/hooks/slack-post-guard.sh` with three rules, `slack-post-guard-test.sh` at 108 assertions, registered on the Bash matcher, on the three Slack MCP write tools, and on `PostToolUse`. The two-target split written into `HOME/repos/.claude/refs/slack.md` and pointed at from `slack-clipboard/SKILL.md`.

### Design decisions
- **The gate is the first thing in the file and `lib.sh` is sourced after it.** Phase 0 made gating a requirement rather than an optimization (230 ms ungated against a 250 ms budget, 27 ms gated), and the prototype it measured sourced `lib.sh` before the predicate. Sourcing after it means a non-Slack Bash call pays one `case` and one jq.
- **One jq spawn on the hot path, not three.** Reading `hook_event_name`, `tool_name` and `tool_input.command` as separate jq calls cost 71 ms on a plain `git status` and failed the 50 ms criterion on its own, with no transcript read at all: jq costs about 23 ms per invocation here. They come back from one call, with the command base64-encoded because it can carry newlines and tabs, decoded only once the gate passes. Measured after: 27 ms against a 5 MB transcript.
- **`tail -n +2` is not in the transcript reader.** Phase 0's prototype dropped the tail's first line because a 4 MB tail can start mid-record. That also drops a whole record from any transcript smaller than the cap, which is 98.4% of them. `fromjson? // empty` already discards the partial line, so the truncation guard was doing nothing but losing data.
- **The prompt extractor is `prompt_id`-first with the corrected selector as the fallback.** Criterion 8 measured the fallback alone at 0 relay and 0 wrapper false authorizations over 1,237 turns; `prompt_id` (identical across every tool call in a turn, per criterion 3's live dump) makes the common case exact instead of positional.
- **RESEND does not run when every recipient is exempt.** The rule text carries no exemption for the pair, and applying it there would deny a second identical `/slack-clipboard` inside the hour. A duplicate into a single-member private channel harms nobody, and Scott's 2026-09-11 ruling on that pair is about friction, not about recipients. Disclosed deviation, see below.
- **`--preview` resolves to the exempt DM rather than to the named target**, because that is where the client sends it (a render sandbox in the caller's own self-DM), and `--print` posts nothing at all and returns an allow before any rule runs.

### Deviations
- **Expiry reclamation is an O_EXCL lock, not the doc's rename.** The doc prescribes "a single atomic rename of a freshly created temp entry over the old path". That rename is atomic and it is not a compare-and-swap: `mv temp path` succeeds whether or not the path still holds the entry the process measured, so every racer that reads the same expired mtime renames and proceeds. Its own acceptance criterion, two concurrent reclaims leaving exactly one allowed, cannot pass in that shape. Renaming the expired entry AWAY is a compare-and-swap and was the first fix here; it still failed 1 round in 30 under 8 racers, because a file that turns out to be someone else's fresh reservation has to be put back and the path is EMPTY for the length of that restore, which a third process's plain O_EXCL create walks straight into. Any scheme that removes a live entry even briefly has that window. The shipped shape never moves the entry: a separate O_EXCL lock admits one reclaimer, which re-reads expiry while holding it. 120 rounds of 8 racers, zero violations.
- **RESEND is scoped to the non-exempt recipient set** (above). The doc's RESEND text names no exemption; this adds one.
- **TARGET and TEST-TEXT apply to `chat_update`, RESEND does not.** The doc exempts `chat_update` in the RESEND paragraph only, and the reasoning given (an edit is the opposite of a resend, and `ChatUpdateRequest` cannot fan out) is RESEND-specific. An edit still names a channel and can still rewrite a body into a test post, so the other two rules run.
- **An unquoted `#channel` denies as a parse failure.** It is a shell comment, so `slack write #engineering hi` runs `slack write` with no arguments and the CLI never sees a target. `lib.sh`'s maskers preserve length, so the target arrives as a run of `\001`; the guard treats that as no target rather than as a name to resolve. Not in the doc, and every fixture in the matrix uses the bare name or a quoted `#name` for the same reason.
- **The write parser keeps accepting flags after the target.** `content` is a `trailing_var_arg` positional, so clap parses flags right up until the first content token. A parser that stops at the target reads `--broadcast`, `--dm-mentioned` and `--edit` as body words, which silently disarms three rules by argument order alone. Caught by the matrix at four failures.

### Tradeoffs
- **`HOME` is the test seam and it is therefore a residual hole**, named rather than patched blind, the same way the doc names the Grep/Glob hole for SECRET. A `HOME=/tmp/x slack write ...` reads an id cache an agent could have written. It denies for every target that cache cannot resolve, it cannot fake the transcript (the harness supplies the path), and the prefix is glaring in the transcript and in `clyde permit log`. Closing it costs the matrix every branch it has: missing cache, schema-old cache, stale cache, ledger races, reclaim, unwritable ledger.
- **A failed send is not retryable until the entry expires**, which is the doc's ruling and is asserted as such. The deny names the exact file to remove.
- **Name matching authorizes on a common word when a channel is named one.** `#general` matches "in general we should". The alternative, requiring the literal channel id, blocks 72% of legitimate posts by the doc's own measurement.
- **The plugin's `slack:write` skill is NOT edited.** It lives in `~/.claude/plugins/cache/tatari-skills/`, outside this repo and overwritten on the next plugin update, so the two-target split went into `refs/slack.md` (in-repo, lint-covered, read whenever Slack work begins) with a pointer from `slack-clipboard/SKILL.md`.

### Break-the-code evidence
Each rule disabled in a scratch copy, matrix re-run against the copy:

```
baseline        pass=108 fail=0
TARGET-off      pass=62  fail=46
TESTTEXT-off    pass=104 fail=4
RESEND-off      pass=101 fail=7
```

### Open questions
- None.

### Observed, not changed
- `HOME/repos/.claude/refs/slack.md` is stale in three places outside this phase's scope: it points at `mcp__slack__conversations_add_message` (a retired tool), at `~/repos/.claude/slack-ids.json` (the cache is `~/.cache/slack/ids.json` now), and at `~/.claude/skills/slack/slack.py` (the retired monolith, now `slack-old`). Recorded rather than fixed: unrequested scope.

## SLACK rework: matching the intent instead of the rule text

Commit: this phase. `slack-post-guard.sh` TARGET rebuilt on two sufficient conditions over a 3-turn window, TEST-TEXT narrowed to a marker line, three parse fixes. Matrix 108 to 123 assertions.

Scott, after reading the acceptance walk: "it sounds like you built something that would annoy the fuck out of me. dont do that. match the intent of this work."

### What the first cut got wrong
The rule text says resolve the target and require it named. I implemented that faithfully and it was the wrong thing, because the rule text rests on an assumption the cache does not support. Replayed against 216 historical posts with their real prompts: **79 denies, and they were the asks.** `message russ to point at valet.test.tatari.dev and enroll` denied. `send a message to ryan` denied. `i didnt ask for a draft. I asked you to send it` denied. `slack write --help` denied.

Two causes, both measurable and neither visible from reading the code:
- **A DM cannot be resolved to a name.** `~/.cache/slack/ids.json`'s `users` map holds 120 DM ids, and `D01TL0BDQ4T`, `D0AH0DP9RJ5`, `D0B8FU6DLKU` and `D01VB7QMKJ7` are all absent from it. So for a DM the rule degenerates into "the prompt must contain the raw `D0...` id", which is precisely the shape the doc priced at 72% of legitimate posts blocked and wrote name matching to avoid. I built the thing the doc warned about and the matrix passed 108 assertions over it, because every fixture used a DM id I had put in the fixture cache myself.
- **A posting task spans turns.** The turn that names the target is followed by `do it`, `yes`, `WAY TOO WORDY`, `did you fucking fix your mess?`. Reading only the current turn throws the authorization away one turn after it is given.

### The fix
- **Two sufficient conditions, either one allows**: the recipient named in the last 3 typed turns (the doc's rule, kept wherever it can actually be evaluated), or a recent typed turn that asks for a Slack post at all. Only failing both denies.
- **A 3-turn window** rather than the current turn, which is what the doc's commit-guard evidence used.
- The word set for "asks for a post" is taken from the 211 posts' own prompts, not invented.

Measured alternative, rejected: require the name when the target IS resolvable and fall back to the posting ask only when it is not. That keeps the wrong-channel protection and costs too much, 19 real denies instead of 9, and the denials it adds include `i didnt ask for a draft. I asked you to send it` and `send the announcement to #engineering` crossposting to a second channel. Name matching survives only as the fast path.

### What this gives up, stated plainly
"The right ask to the wrong channel" now passes. A live posting task authorizes a post to a channel the window does not name, and a `dm_mentioned` fan-out past the named channel. No incident in the corpus is that shape: all three are an unasked post, a duplicate, or a test post. The three matrix fixtures that asserted the old behavior were flipped to allow, with the reason written at each one.

### Three parse bugs the replay found
- `slack write --help` denied 20 times: the no-target check ran before the posts-nothing check. Reordered.
- `slack write --help 2>&1 | head -40` read the `2` of `2>&1` as the target. Redirects are stripped before tokenizing now, the same `sed` the LN rule uses.
- `slack write '@scott.idler'` denied: Scott's own DM by handle was not an exempt spelling. The exempt set now carries the handle spellings alongside the two literal ids.

### TEST-TEXT narrowed
Matching test/verify anywhere in the first line denied two real posts whose first line was a 180-character sentence about a test environment: "marquee DID already ship its own MCP-auth path: live on test and prod" and "the host the cli defaults to just isnt deployed yet, only the test one is". The incident is `**MCP write test**`, a short line that IS the marker, so the word now counts when the first line is short enough to be a marker or when it opens the line.

### The lesson worth keeping
A guard's matrix cannot tell you whether the guard matches its intent, because the fixtures are written by the same hand and the same assumptions as the rule. 108 assertions passed over a rule that denied a third of Scott's real posts. The replay against the actual corpus is the test that bites, and it belongs in the acceptance criteria for every rule whose intent includes "do not get in the way", not just for the one where the doc happened to price it.

### Open questions
- None from this rework. The two open items are unchanged: the INGEST wrapper bypass, and whether the SECRET jq allowlist gets a captured-into-a-variable carve-out.

## Phase 2: Schema 2 and the migration gate

### Design decisions

- **The migration is a shared `ensure_schema_current` seam called by every path
  that can reach `fill_users`, not a schema arm bolted onto each index's
  staleness check** -- `mention.rs:CacheLookup::ensure_schema_current`. The
  design names `usergroups_stale` as the site needing a schema arm and says the
  schema-stale case routes to `refresh()`. Implementing only that would have
  left the hole open, because `fill_users` is the sole `schema` STAMPER and it
  is reachable from three places, only one of which the design enumerates:
  `ensure_users_fresh` (the `users` verb), `MentionLookup::user` (write-path
  mentions), and `DecodeLookup::user` (read/search decode). A `slack write`
  carrying one `@mention` would otherwise stamp the scalar current and strand
  `subteams` empty for 24h -- the identical order-dependence bug, entering by a
  door the design's table does not list. All three now migrate through the seam.
- **The channel paths are deliberately NOT gated** --
  `mention.rs:DecodeLookup::user` carries the note. `fill_channels` never stamps
  `schema`, so a channel resolution cannot strand another index, and forcing a
  12-request refresh to render one `<#C…>` span is over-reach. Every READER of
  `subteams` is gated, so a cache left at the old schema by a channel-only run
  still cannot render a sparse group column -- it just migrates later, on the
  first run that actually asks a group question.
- **`usergroups_stale` and `users_stale` keep their own schema arms as
  fail-safes**, even though `ensure_schema_current` runs first and makes them
  redundant. A future caller that forgets the seam then reads STALE and fills:
  wasteful, but correct, rather than serving a sparse column. The design asked
  for the arm on the METHOD (`usergroups_stale`) rather than the free function,
  and that is where it is -- the free `usergroups_stale(synced_at, now)` takes
  two scalars and structurally cannot see a schema, which is why the index had
  no schema arm at all before this phase. Pinned by
  `usergroups_stale_method_reads_schema_where_the_free_fn_cannot`.

### Deviations

- **A brand-new cache is NOT treated as schema-stale.** The design says "a
  schema-stale cache triggers ONE full `refresh()`" and defines staleness as
  `schema < CURRENT_SCHEMA`. Read literally that also catches a never-written
  cache, whose `schema` defaults to `0` -- so every fresh install would do a
  three-index, 12-request refresh on its first `@mention`, discarding the
  laziness this module is built around (the cache is not even loaded until the
  first sigil token is seen). `schema_stale` therefore additionally requires at
  least one stamped watermark, which is what distinguishes "written by an older
  binary" from "never written".

  This does not reopen the hole the design closed. The order-dependence bug
  needs an index with a FRESH watermark sitting behind a schema flag someone
  else already cleared; with no watermark set at all, every per-index gate reads
  stale on its own terms and fills lazily, so no index can be left
  fresh-but-empty. Verified by the cold-cache tests, which still assert exactly
  one `usergroups.list` and no `users.list`.
- **The schema decision is made once per run, against the cache as FOUND** --
  `schema_checked_this_run` is set BEFORE the staleness test, not only when a
  migration fires. Found by a test failure rather than by reading: a run mutates
  the very fields `schema_stale` reads. A lazy usergroup fill stamps
  `usergroups_synced_at` while leaving `schema` at its old value (only
  `upsert_full_user_sync` stamps), so the SECOND lookup in the same run saw "a
  watermark, and an old schema" and diagnosed the run's own work as a migration,
  firing a full refresh mid-run. Evaluating once keeps the question "was this
  file written by an older binary", which is a property of the file on entry and
  cannot change mid-run.
- **Phase 2's order-independence criterion is asserted as a UNIT test over both
  entry points, not at the CLI.** The criterion says `slack users idler` first
  and `slack usergroups` first must both end identically. At Phase 2 that is not
  yet expressible at the CLI: `slack usergroups` still reads live and touches
  the cache only under `--members`, so it cannot trigger the gate at all until
  Phase 3 makes the verb cache-first.
  `schema_migration_is_order_independent_across_both_entry_points` drives the
  two real entry points directly (`ensure_users_fresh` and `usergroup_handle`)
  from an identical schema-stale fixture and asserts both orderings end with
  `schema == CURRENT_SCHEMA`, populated `profiles`, AND populated `subteams`
  carrying membership. The CLI-level both-orderings check is AC4 and is run at
  finalization, after Phase 3.

### Tradeoffs

- **Nine test fixtures updated vs. exempting old fixtures from the gate.**
  Bumping the schema made every fixture seeded at the old schema migrate, which
  their mocks did not cover. Each was classified rather than blanket-patched:
  fixtures whose intent is "an already-current cache exercising the watermark
  path" now say `schema = CURRENT_SCHEMA` explicitly (their intent is unchanged,
  it is just no longer implicit), and the two whose intent IS the migration
  (`a_profiles_map_missing_real_name_refills_rather_than_rendering_sparse`,
  `second_run_after_migration_issues_zero_requests`) now mock the full refresh.
  The alternative -- a test-only escape hatch on the gate -- would mean the
  production migration path is never exercised by the suite.
- **`second_run_after_migration_issues_zero_requests` was given a genuine
  pre-migration fixture.** It previously seeded an EMPTY cache, which under the
  refined rule is a fresh install rather than a migration -- so the test would
  have stopped testing what its name claims. It now seeds a stamped watermark
  plus an out-of-date `schema`.

### Open questions

- None.

### Success criteria: recorded results

`otto ci` green, exit 0, 472 tests passed. Live criteria run against a
